articles.title: Why and how US and Canadian energy markets are so deeply intertwined
articles.author: Stefano Tijerina, Senior Lecturer of Management, University of Maine
paras: The 50% tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump’s administration on imports from Canada in July 2026, and the reciprocal 50% tariffs imposed by Prime Minister Mark Carney’s administration on imports to Canada from the U.S. a month later, do not include oil and natural gas. Electricity and some petroleum products were also left out, although they remain subject to a 10% tariff imposed in 2025.

That’s because the two countries’ energy systems and markets are so intertwined that tariffs would devastate both economies. Canada is the biggest supplier of foreign petroleum to the United States, supplying half of all its petroleum imports. It is also the only direct foreign supplier of electricity to the U.S., with 34 major transmission points moving electricity from Canada south across the border.
In truth, Canada could shut down those power links and leave thousands of Americans in the dark, as Ontario provincial Premier Doug Ford threatened in August 2026.

But researchers like me, who study the historical links that have shaped Canadian and U.S. business relations, know that over the past 50 years Canada has expanded its energy production with one specific goal: serving U.S. consumption. In 2024, 84% of Canadian oil production and 76% of Canadian electricity production were exported to the U.S. Without American buyers, there is no real energy market in Canada.

Since the second half of the 19th century, energy generated on both sides of the border – and across them – has connected the two nations. The Great Lakes Basin was the hydraulic center of energy interconnectivity, as both nations shared the energy generated by Niagara Falls and the St. Lawrence River.

During the early stages of World War II, even before the U.S. entered the fight, Canada and the U.S. started to integrate their energy systems. That work was part of joint security efforts to protect North America through the integration of defense manufacturing production systems.

The Ogdensburg Declaration of 1940 and the 1941 Hyde Park Declaration consolidated and formalized the strategic economic and military cooperation between the two countries and set the foundations for future collaboration.
From cooperation to integration
After the war, Canadian and U.S. businesses liked the idea of sharing production and manufacturing operations, even beyond war-related work.

Nevertheless, manufacturing on both sides of the border went back to prewar ways of producing things domestically. Nationalist voices opposed the idea of further integrating the Canadian and U.S. economies.

Less than two decades after the war ended, though, the two nations signed the Auto Pact of 1965, which eliminated tariffs on cars, trucks and automotive parts. Canadian parts manufacturers could compete directly with those based in the U.S., all to serve U.S. automakers.
This initial experiment in free trade revealed to businesses on both sides of the border that supply chain integration could benefit other production and service industries.

By 1989, the two countries had signed a full-scale free trade agreement that removed tariffs for goods crossing the border in either direction. That opened the door for more closely integrating their energy markets too.

In 1992, a U.S. federal law changed a wide swath of regulations over the country’s energy markets. Some of the provisions allowed Canadian companies to sell excess energy to the U.S., and two years later the North American Free Trade Agreement brought Mexico into the relationship too.
NAFTA integrated the production, processing and distribution of thousands of goods and services across all three countries.

But it was the interconnection of energy infrastructure that turned the Canadian and U.S. economies into one single energy market. Today, four major U.S. electrical grids depend on imported power from Canada: those serving the six New England states, New York state, 15 states across the Midwest and the South, and California.

Moreover, there are more than 40 natural gas and petroleum liquids pipelines connecting Canada with the United States. And although energy products move back and forth across the border, the U.S. has an energy trade deficit with Canada. Much of the U.S. economy runs on Canadian energy, and much of Canada’s energy production is sold to the U.S.
The current reality on the ground shows an integrated energy system between the two nations: something very difficult and costly to untangle, and a process that would take decades to reengineer.
Today, those links form the basis for very tight integration between the two countries’ business and industrial marketplaces.
For example, Maine, where I live and work, gets close to 30% of its electricity from Canada.
The state’s northern electrical grid is run by the New Brunswick Power Corp., owned by the province of New Brunswick, which serves close to 60,000 Mainers.

Today, Maine’s electric grid is owned mostly by foreign interests, including ENMAX, the municipally owned utilities corporation of Calgary, Alberta, and the owner of Versant Power, which serves 16% of Maine’s market. And 80% is served by Central Maine Power, which is owned by Iberdrola from Spain.

Canadian energy reaches deeper into the U.S., too. In 2025, Hydro-Quebec, a company that generates electricity from dams across the province of Quebec, secured a deal with local regulators to use Maine as a corridor to supply clean energy to Massachusetts. Hydro-Quebec is owned by the government of the province of Quebec.
The bilateral integration of energy infrastructure over the past 30-plus years explains why this sector was exempt from the most recent tariffs.

Stefano Tijerina does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: How candidates are (quietly) talking about climate change – 3 election strategies you’ll see across the US
articles.author: Geoffrey Henderson, Assistant Professor, School for Environment and Sustainability, University of Michigan
paras: Amid wars, inflation, emerging risks from artificial intelligence and threats to democracy, Americans have a lot to be worried about these days. But polls show the majority of voters in 2026 are also concerned about climate change as temperatures and disaster risks rise.
So why are fewer candidates talking openly about climate change in their midterm election campaigns than just a few years ago?
At the University of Michigan’s School for Environment and Sustainability, we study climate communication and are following how Democratic candidates are discussing climate change in their campaigns.

Democratic candidates seem to agree on one strategy: campaign centrally on affordability, emphasizing how ordinary people are struggling to afford to fill up their cars, pay their electric bills and insure their homes against hurricanes and wildfires. It’s part of a concerted effort to make the election a referendum on Republicans’ support for the Trump administration’s contributions to inflation, such as tariffs and the Iran war.

Fossil fuel industry interests have long sought to polarize the public over the phrase “climate change.” As one of us, Geoffrey Henderson, discusses in his new book, “Getting to Work on Climate Policy: The Strategy of Labor-Environmental Coalitions,” campaigns pitting economic concerns against environmental ones have made it harder to build support for policies meant to slow climate change.
When it comes to talking about climate change today, three distinct camps of Democratic candidates and officeholders reveal three different strategies.
The energy populists talk a lot about lowering energy prices for consumers but very little about either climate change or fossil fuels.

Many have been painting data centers, rather than fossil fuel producers, as villains. Candidates often use messages focused on how utilities and data centers are raising voters’ electric rates. They propose measures to lower these costs, like requiring data centers to bring their own energy sources onto the grid.

In North Carolina, former governor Roy Cooper, now running for U.S. Senate, emphasizes lowering energy and utility costs. Sherrod Brown of Ohio, campaigning to return to the Senate, argues that his opponent’s votes in favor of data centers have led to “higher electric rates.”

Discussing energy affordability, without directly calling out the risks to the climate from burning fossil fuels or advocating for more renewable energy, aligns with the argument that climate change messages can alienate swing voters, who prioritize affordability.

If energy populists are elected, they could become silent backers of climate policies to reduce greenhouse gas emissions – both Brown and Cooper have a record of supporting renewable energy – or obstacles to climate policies.
Not all Democrats, even in battleground states, think climate change should fade into the background this election. However, few are as outspoken today as they were in the past.

In Massachusetts, Sen. Ed Markey’s website pledges that he will champion “bold action to invest in clean energy” if reelected in November. In Maine, Senate candidate Troy Jackson asserts that politicians should not pit working-class people against renewable energy, casting the climate-versus-affordability debate as a false choice.

Rhode Island’s Sheldon Whitehouse, one of the Senate’s most outspoken supporters of pro-climate policies, contends that candidates should link higher costs to climate change, such as increased home insurance costs due to hurricane risk. He also points to President Donald Trump’s blockade of the cheapest energy sources – namely, solar and wind power – which he attributes to fossil fuel industry influence.

If elected, these candidates’ messages suggest they will pursue policies that help reduce U.S. contributions to climate change. However, they may need to convince independent voters that their focus on climate change will not overshadow their attention to other challenges.
The all-of-the-above proponents

Another group of candidates wants to have it both ways. They call for actions that can respond to climate change and rapidly build out renewable energy, while also promising cheaper gasoline and more fossil fuel jobs. Scientists warn that more fossil fuel use cuts against global climate goals.

Unlike the other camps, this group does not identify villains in their narrative. These candidates are following the script from the Obama administration, whose “all of the above” energy strategy espoused continued fossil fuel use alongside policies to reduce planet-warming emissions.

In Iowa, U.S. Senate candidate Josh Turek hosted a roundtable in April 2026 on how climate-fueled extreme weather is raising insurance costs. But he has also focused on lowering the cost of gasoline and diesel. James Talarico, campaigning for the Senate in Texas, has similarly promised to fight climate change by boosting renewable energy while lowering costs by promoting all energy sources.

These candidates may be trying to signal their potential to support climate policies while respecting their states’ cultural connections to fossil fuels. Turek and Talarico are both running in states with abundant wind power.
Where are the voters on this issue?
Studies from the U.S. and Germany find that politicians usually underestimate public support for efforts to address climate change.
So how well do candidates’ platforms represent today’s voters?

Yale’s spring 2026 survey found that 49% of voters believe global warming should be a high priority for Congress and the president. But 70% of moderate or conservative Democrats share this view, alongside 84% of liberal Democrats. Even 1 in 3 liberal-to-moderate Republicans considers the climate a high priority.

Yet polling also suggests that other issues, such as the increasing cost of living, are even more important to many voters. This data suggests that pro-climate messages could appeal to swing voters most strongly if climate policies are seen as complementary to affordability.

Still, a recent survey shows that voters open to Democratic candidates are more likely to support a candidate who prioritizes climate change. Climate messaging may especially resonate with young voters. Over a third of those ages 18 to 29 in a recent Harvard Youth Poll considered climate change an urgent national crisis. Young Republicans are more supportive of addressing climate change than their older counterparts.

While many shifts in the way candidates talk about climate policy have little impact on people’s willingness to participate in collective efforts to address it, messages emphasizing cost savings durably increase support for renewable energy across party lines. Voters’ current concerns about inflation could make climate messages involving affordability especially effective in 2026, though the impact of these messages may vary from state to state.
Retail politics and the way forward

These different approaches reflect the Democratic Party’s efforts to build a “big tent” that can attract voters with a wide range of views and priorities. Yet Democrats are generally coalescing around a message designed to appeal to working-class voters: that Trump and the Republicans are raising your cost of living.
November’s midterm elections will offer some insight into whether Democrats’ energy affordability message will resonate in the 2028 presidential election.
Geoffrey Henderson has worked on a project that received funding from the National Science Foundation.
Nathaniel Geiger has received funding from the National Science Foundation.

articles.title: Pennsylvania’s aging prisons weren’t built for today’s extreme weather – leaving women and seniors especially at risk of illness and death
articles.author: Jaquelyn Jahn, Assistant Professor of Epidemiology, Drexel University
paras: When outdoor temperatures spike to 103 degrees Fahrenheit (39 degrees Celsius), or drop to -9 F (-23 C), like they did across Pennsylvania last year, people locked up in jails and prisons cannot simply turn on the air conditioning or find a public warming center.
For several years, people in custody, advocates and local media have sounded the alarm about the dangers posed by extreme temperatures in Pennsylvania’s state prisons.

Conditions inside Pennsylvania’s prisons have been described as a sauna during a summer heat wave and bitterly cold in the winter, especially when heating systems have malfunctioned. Amy McBride, a woman in her early 60s incarcerated at MCI Muncy, told the Prison Journalism Project, “I tend to wear two to three layers of pants and four to six layers of shirts (in winter), sometimes with my jacket and coat over them.”

I am an epidemiologist who studies the health of incarcerated people. My colleagues and I put numbers to these warnings in a recent study. We found that extreme hot and cold temperatures were associated with higher rates of deaths, infirmary admissions and transfers to external medical facilities among imprisoned people in Pennsylvania over the past 20 years.

While these temperature hazards are not unique to Pennsylvania, several factors make this issue a particular concern for the state. Pennsylvania has the nation’s sixth-largest prison population among U.S. states. Nearly 40,000 people are confined in Pennsylvania prisons.

Furthermore, most of Pennsylvania’s state prison facilities were built in the 1990s or earlier, when weather patterns were not so extreme. Some, including the state correctional institutions in Cambridge Springs, Dallas, Laurel Highlands, Muncy, Waymart and Huntingdon, the oldest continuously running correctional facility in Pennsylvania, have partial or very limited air conditioning. This means they have air conditioning in some buildings or units, such as nursing care areas, and not others.

Previous research also suggests that while hot temperatures pose risks to incarcerated people across the country, those incarcerated in the Northeast have experienced some of the greatest increases in heat-related mortality risk since 2001.
Prison healthcare systems under strain

Even under normal weather conditions, prison healthcare systems are highly strained. People in prison are more likely than the general population to have chronic medical conditions such as heart disease, and the state’s prison population is getting older, which increases its medical needs and expenses. The average age at prison admission has increased from 31 in 2000 to 38 in 2023.
The average cost for medications alone for adults over 50 in the state’s prison is US$3,357 per person per year. That’s 53% more than costs for younger incarcerated adults.

The state prison system experiences chronic staffing shortages of corrections officers, nurses and physicians. Some facilities have experienced vacancy rates of medical staff of nearly 40%. Shortages of corrections officers result in greater restrictions on the movement of incarcerated people, who then have less access to health appointments, group therapy and other programming. This can be especially difficult for older incarcerated people and those who have been incarcerated for long periods of time, because they have greater medical needs and are often more isolated from loved ones.

Constitutional protections against cruel and unusual punishment prohibit deliberate indifference to prisoners’ medical needs. But in addition to staffing shortages and other administrative challenges with healthcare delivery in prisons, incarcerated people also face financial barriers.

In Pennsylvania, they must pay a $5 copay per visit to receive medical treatment that is determined by the Department of Correction to not be an emergency. This may sound low but is substantial in the context of wages that range from 23 cents to 50 cents per hour.
Incarcerated women may face higher heat risks

One unexpected finding from our analysis was that women in Pennsylvania state prisons experienced greater increases in rates of infirmary visits and transfers to external medical facilities on and after extremely hot days than men.

This was unexpected because previous studies haven’t consistently shown that women are more vulnerable to heat-related health risks. But these studies were conducted in the general population, not among people in prison.

Incarcerated people experience what medical researchers call “accelerated aging” because of the stressors they experience during and prior to incarceration. This means their biologic age is ahead of their chronological age. They are more likely to experience menopause, cancer and chronic disease at a younger age than would typically be expected.
Hot flashes and night sweats are common symptoms of menopause that can become life threatening during extreme heat events and when cooling, hydration and hormone therapy are limited or unavailable.
Preparing for a warmer climate

Our research found that extreme heat and extreme cold increase the demands on an already strained system of prison operations and healthcare delivery. These demands will likely only get worse as extreme temperatures continue to intensify.

We believe climate resilience planning will require improvements in prison conditions, improvements in prison healthcare systems, and policy efforts to reduce the number of people – particularly older adults – who are incarcerated.
Jaquelyn Jahn receives funding from the National Institutes of Health, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Arnold Ventures, and the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation.

articles.title: For centuries, bird migration was a mystery – a tech revolution is changing that, and could help save these amazing creatures
articles.author: Peter P. Marra, Dean of The Earth Commons, Professor of Biology and the Environment, Georgetown University
paras: For more than 2,000 years, scientists have scratched their heads over one of the most basic mysteries of the natural world: Where do birds go?

Billions of birds appear and disappear with the seasons every year. Early naturalists offered explanations for the disappearances that today seem fantastical: Birds transformed into other species, one theory went. Others suggested they hibernated underwater or even migrated to the moon.
The truth, that these small animals were traveling thousands of miles across the planet, must once have seemed just as improbable.

Then, in the early 1800s, dramatic evidence emerged supporting the theory of migration. White storks began appearing in Germany with African arrows embedded in their bodies. These birds became known as pfeilstörche, or “arrow storks.” They provided compelling evidence that birds disappearing from Europe were traveling all the way to Africa and back.
Almost two centuries later, scientists are still asking the same question, but our ability to answer it has been transformed.

For most of ornithological history, scientists understood migration through brief glimpses of a bird, a specimen collected somewhere else, or the rare instance of a banded bird recovered hundreds or thousands of miles from where it had been marked. From these fragments of intelligence, scientists reconstructed journeys that took place largely beyond their view.
Today, it’s possible to see the journeys themselves, almost in real time.
A century of following birds

Bird banding was the first tool used to attempt a systematic approach to connect these fragments of information. Since the early 1900s, researchers have placed uniquely numbered metal bands on birds and hoped someone, somewhere, would encounter them again.

Of more than 79 million birds banded, only about 6.5 million have been recovered. That generally told scientists just two things: where a bird was banded and where it was encountered again. Everything between them remained invisible.
Over the past quarter-century or so, the tools used to determine where birds go have changed dramatically.

Tracking devices can now be carried by increasingly smaller birds, recording their movements and communicating with land-based receivers or satellites orbiting the earth. Testing stable isotopes in feathers and other tissues can reveal where a bird originated. Genetic testing can distinguish populations.
At the same time, the extraordinary growth of bird-watching and citizen science has created another revolution.

Millions of observations by bird-watchers submitted to eBird, an online database to record the birds they see, show the distribution and abundance of birds across a continent throughout the year in ways early ornithologists could scarcely have imagined.
Collectively, these methods open an extraordinary new window into migratory birds and one of nature’s most remarkable behaviors: migration.
Discovering unknown migrations
More than 70% of North American bird species are migratory. Yet scientists have known surprisingly little about where specific populations go.

A species like the American robin may breed across thousands of miles of North America, with different breeding populations migrating to entirely different places for the winter. Birds breeding in one part of the continent may travel one route and encounter one set of environmental conditions, while members of the same species experience a completely different set of conditions along another route.

These connections between where a bird breeds and where it spends the winter is called migratory connectivity. They are critical for understanding everything from the consequences of climate change on birds to how avian pathogens and diseases spread, to a species’ basic ecology.

We are ornithologists and conservation scientists who have spent almost 15 years along with a team of contributors compiling this rapidly expanding knowledge on bird movement into The Atlas of North America’s Migratory Birds. The atlas, being published on Nov. 3, 2026, by Princeton University Press, covers the latest information on seasonal movements for nearly 600 species and combines a century of bird-banding data with eBird observations, tracking studies, stable isotope testing, genetics and other sources of information.
What emerges is a picture of migratory birds that is both more complicated and more remarkable than the simple arrows pointing between breeding and wintering ranges on a map.

Consider the yellow-billed cuckoo. These birds breed over a wide range of the eastern two-thirds of the U.S. but migrate to a relatively small wintering area in the Gran Chaco region of northern Argentina, Paraguay and southern Bolivia.
In contrast, peregrine falcons that breed in Alaska migrate almost directly south, dispersing across the Americas to wintering grounds that extend as far as southern South America.
Discoveries like these are accumulating rapidly. Collectively, they amount to a renaissance in our understanding of animal movement never before imagined.
The more clearly scientists can follow individual birds and populations across the planet, the more extraordinary these species can seem.

Migratory birds such as the arctic tern and northern wheatear cross oceans, deserts and mountain ranges. Some, like the bar-tailed godwits, fly thousands of miles without stopping. Others, like the American redstart, return year after year to remarkably precise breeding and wintering locations.
They navigate landscapes and respond to winds, weather, food and environmental conditions across enormous geographic scales.

We see these species and their migrations as among evolution’s great living masterpieces. That’s why we combined science with natural history and artist John Anderton’s extraordinary illustrations of the birds themselves. The maps allow us to see where birds travel, and the art brings the species to life.
Together, they make visible something that humans could only imagine for most of our history.
North America has lost about 3 billion birds during the past half-century, and many migratory species continue to decline.

To understand why a population is declining and help save it, researchers need to understand the species’ entire annual cycle: its critical stopover habitats, wintering grounds and threats along its migration routes.

For much of the history of ornithology, scientists studied birds primarily during their breeding season. That made practical sense. Birds are conspicuous then – singing, defending territories, building nests and raising young.

But a migratory bird may spend only a few months of its life in its breeding grounds. Conditions such as weather, food availability and habitat quality encountered during migration can determine whether an individual survives to breed again.

Drought thousands of miles away can affect a bird’s condition months later. American redstarts depart later after dry winters and produce fewer young. Declining horseshoe crab populations in Delaware Bay have reduced food availability for migrating red knots, contributing to lower survival.
All of this knowledge has accumulated because people value birds and have devoted enormous time and effort to understanding them.

For more than a century, thousands of bird-banders have woken up before the crack of dawn to set traps, carefully place bands on birds’ legs and release them, often knowing the chances of ever learning what happened to those individuals were exceedingly small.

More recently, tracking technology has allowed researchers to follow individual birds across continents and oceans. Those tracks exist because scientists, students, technicians and others have spent countless hours attaching and recovering tags, and contributing and sharing their data.
Today, millions of bird-watchers contribute observations that, thanks to advances in data science, allow us to watch migration unfold across an entire continent.
We have spent much of our careers documenting the decline of birds, and we know the challenges facing migratory species are formidable. But we also have hope for these creatures’ survival.

Scientists today know more about where migratory birds go, how populations are connected and what they encounter along the way than at any previous point in history. That knowledge is helping to identify where conservation efforts can make a difference for the future.

articles.title: Americans want electric cars – they just can’t find them
articles.author: John Paul Helveston, Associate Professor of Engineering Management and Systems Engineering, George Washington University
paras: Within three months of the U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb. 28, 2026, the average price of gasoline for American drivers climbed from US$2.94 to $4.35 a gallon. If there was ever a moment for Americans to switch to electric vehicles, this was it.
From March to May 2026, in fact, sales of hybrid electric vehicles were 18% higher than over the same months in 2025.

But sales of fully electric vehicles were 16% lower from March to May 2026 compared with the same months in 2025. Some observers took that as evidence that high gas prices alone wouldn’t push Americans toward fully electric cars, but that conclusion misses half the story.

I study car buyers and their preferences, and there is an important distinction between what consumers want and what they can actually buy. Sales reveal what cars people actually bought, but not necessarily what they actually wanted.
When the supply of some kinds of cars can’t keep up with demand, prices rise, and that’s exactly what happened for electric vehicles in 2026.
In 2026, hybrids and all-electric vehicles faced the same jump in demand from the oil crisis. While there were plenty of hybrids available to meet that demand, the same was not true for EVs.

Hybrid production had been growing for years, led by Toyota, which sells about half of the hybrids bought in the United States. As a result, even as sales surged, hybrid inventories on dealer lots were 19% higher in March 2026 than they had been a year earlier.

However, EV production had been in retreat since the tax and spending law President Donald Trump signed in July 2025 ended federal tax credits for EVs. Buyers had been able to get up to $7,500 for new EVs and $4,000 for used ones, but that ended after Sept. 30, 2025.

Automakers responded by cutting back their EV production. General Motors laid off more than 3,400 workers at its EV and battery plants and shifted its Tennessee plant to make batteries for energy storage, not cars. Ford wrote off $19.5 billion from its EV business, ended production of the all-electric F-150 Lightning and converted a Tennessee EV plant to build gas-powered trucks.

Buyers, for their part, rushed to beat the tax credit deadline, pushing EVs to 11.3% of new vehicle sales in September 2025. But by November 2025, after the tax credits ended, their share dropped to 4.3%.

As 2026 progressed and gas prices began to rise, so did EV demand. New EV inventories declined, shrinking from about 130 days of supply in the first quarter of 2026 to 78 days by August – just two days above the supply level of gas-burning cars.

Discounts on new EV models shrank too. My analysis of online listings from marketcheck.com shows the median new EV was listed 9.8% below sticker price in February. By April, the median discount was 6.6%, and 4.7% in June. That’s a sign that dealers saw rising demand, not inventory to clear.
A run on used electric vehicles

Before the war, prices for used electric vehicles were still drifting down in the wake of the expired used EV federal tax credit. After the war began, they climbed 13% through late June 2026. For a typical used electric vehicle, that’s about $3,500 more.

Other data sources point in the same direction. Recurrent, a company that reports on batteries and used EVs, found that the price of a used 2023 Chevrolet Bolt rose almost 20% from January to June 2026.
And inventories of used electric vehicles dropped too, with only 31 days of supply in May, 23% below the year before.
None of this means the electric vehicle market is healthy. High prices and uncertain access to charging stations are real stumbling blocks for people who are thinking about buying an EV.

But the data doesn’t support the claim that electric vehicle sales stalled in 2026 because Americans don’t want them. Rather, the sales stalled because there weren’t enough EVs available to buy – and there were plenty of hybrids as an alternative.
The distinction matters because automakers have treated a change in the policy landscape as a change in consumer demand, leading to shortages with real costs.
The average new car now sells for about $50,000 and the average new electric vehicle for about $55,000, according to Kelley Blue Book, a company that tracks car prices.

The current situation leaves drivers exposed to the volatility of oil prices with fewer alternatives. The U.S. is the world’s largest oil producer, yet a war in the Persian Gulf raised gas prices significantly in just three months. Oil trades on a global market, so American drivers pay global prices.
Seven months into the war, the pressure on drivers is still going full throttle. Oil was still above $100 a barrel in mid-October, and diesel hit a record $6.52 a gallon on Sept. 22.
Electric vehicle sales haven’t caught up. Argonne’s data show 86,000 of them sold in August, fewer than the 101,000 sold in May, while hybrid sales stayed above 216,000 a month all summer.
Rather than move to increase electric vehicle supply and make them more affordable, federal policy continues to hinder the U.S. electric vehicle sector.

The fuel economy rule released Sept. 28, 2026, loosens efficiency requirements for gas-powered vehicles and in 2028 ends a system that let automakers that beat the standards – mostly EV makers – earn credits for exceeding them and sell those to automakers that fell short. That means automakers will have fewer regulatory incentives to produce EVs going forward.

Regulators say buyers will save $1,289 on the purchase price of a new gas-powered vehicle from reduced engineering and manufacturing costs to make less efficient engines. But the same analysis estimates drivers will spend about $1,600 more on gas over the life of the car, and that’s using fuel price forecasts well below today’s prices. Economists say the administration’s math does not properly account for those fuel costs.

The U.S. has also effectively shut out Chinese automakers, even though nearly three-quarters of the world’s electric cars are built in China. In 2024, Chinese car buyers could choose from over 130 EV models priced under $40,000; American buyers had just four EV models under that threshold. Beyond tariffs of more than 100% on EVs made in China, a Commerce Department rule bars cars from Chinese-linked automakers starting with model year 2027, even if they are built in the U.S. A bill pending in Congress would widen the ban, blocking Chinese investment in U.S. auto factories altogether.

As long as gas stays expensive, the gap between the electric vehicles Americans want and the electric vehicles dealers can sell them is likely to remain. Decisions such as ending the tax credit, rolling back fuel economy standards and banning Chinese technology all make it harder to build them, which means Americans will continue to have fewer affordable electric vehicles to choose from.
John Paul Helveston receives funding from the U.S. Department of Energy, U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, and the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation.

articles.title: Rabbits were a medieval royal luxury in England – until the Black Death made them commonplace
articles.author: Alex Brown, Associate Professor of Medieval History, Durham University
paras: The European rabbit is a common sight in the British countryside today. Yet it was not always so. They are not native to the British Isles and are one of the most devastating invasive species.

The early history of rabbits in the British Isles tells the captivating story of social change in medieval England. From a rare luxury gifted by kings and the Norman aristocracy, rabbits became more commonplace after the living standards of the poor improved in the years after the Black Death (1346 to 1353).
The satirical depictions of rabbits found in medieval books reveal a gallows humour for social inversion that would not feel out of place today.

Once thought to have been introduced by the Normans, archaeologists have since uncovered a rabbit bone from Roman Britain. However, documentary evidence of rabbits in the British Isles has only been found from the Norman period onwards.

One of the earliest references survives from the Scilly Isles in the form of a tithe, which was a tenth of produce given to the church as an offering. In 1176, the landowner Richard de Wyka admitted that he had withheld paying tithes on his rabbits because he had believed that “tithes were not payable on things of this kind”. His confusion suggests that rabbits were a novelty.

Rabbits continued to be sufficiently rare to warrant the king’s care and attention in the 1200s. In 1235, Henry III gave a gift of ten live rabbits to Geoffrey Despenser, the English landowner and Lord of Martley in Worcestershire, out of his park at Guildford.

A few years later, the king sent men to catch 30 or 40 rabbits in his Guildford park. They were told only to collect them if the warren was well stocked, indicating that the king didn’t want the colony to be depleted.

At the time, rabbits were kept for their meat and fur. Henry III sent out orders for the supply of venison, boars, fish, swans, peacocks, hens, eggs, and hares for various feasts in the early 13th century. It had not been until his Christmas feast of 1240 that he added rabbits to his requisition list.

Rabbits were an expensive delicacy, costing four or five times as much as chickens. Their owners guarded their warrens against poaching and predators to the point that watchtowers and stone lodges were built to protect them.

Yet rabbits did not remain the preserve of the aristocracy. The Black Death (1346 to 1353), which killed between a third and two-thirds of the European population, led to improving living standards for the survivors. Land became more freely available. Labourers could also charge more for their work. And many adopted the lifestyles of those higher up the social ladder.

Legislation was introduced in 1363 to restrict what people could wear according to their social status. Its introduction was explained because of “the excess of dress of people beyond their estate, to the very great destruction and impoverishment of the land.”
Rabbits reflected this social change. They became more commonplace during the 14th and 15th centuries as their meat was eaten by wealthier peasants and their furs worn by aspiring craftsmen.

The fur of the common grey rabbit was used for warmth, but some warrens specialised in rarer silver-grey or black rabbits. Rabbits were still fit for a king and Henry VII had night attire tailored with black rabbit fur.

As rabbit numbers increased through breeding, so too did the number of complaints about the destruction caused by them. Manorial accounts included repeated protests about the loss of crops and damage to land caused by the lord’s rabbits.

At the same time, hunting rabbits and other game was seen as potentially subversive. In 1390, following the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381, parliament introduced legislation against poaching and hunting by labourers and artisans. It was feared that, under the guise of hunting, such people would “make plots and conspiracies of rebellion” against the king.

The king consented to the legislation, extending the ban to the use of “hounds and ferrets, hays, nets, hair-pipes, cords and all other devices to take or destroy beasts of the forest, hares or rabbits, or other sport of gentlefolk”.

Rabbits and hares also reveal the satirical humour of medieval society. The Killer Rabbit of Caerbannog, the fictional and deceptively deadly rabbit from Monty Python and the Holy Grail (1975), is but a modern adaptation of this ironic imagery associated with medieval rabbits.

Rabbits adorn the margins of medieval manuscripts. Playful portrayals of rabbits jousting on the backs of snails point to a gentle self-mockery that pervades medieval culture – in this case of chivalric ideals. More in line with the killer rabbit myth, some went even further, depicting rabbits as violently attacking people and seeking retribution.

The Smithfield Decretals, a manuscript illuminated in London in the 1340s, contains one of the most elaborate of such examples. In it, rabbits are portrayed as turning the tables on their hunters, capturing them, holding them trial, and then executing their human and greyhound hunters.

Such examples fit well within the medieval culture of inverting society – the world turned upside down – for comedic relief. Similar examples include the practice of electing a boy as the bishop for the day in Durham or electing a “lord of misrule” during May Day games.
By 1555 the Swiss naturalist Conrad Gesner could write that “there are few countries wherein coneys (rabbits) do not breed, but the most plenty of all is in England”.
Alex Brown is currently the Principal Investigator of a Leverhulme Trust funded project on 'Modelling the Black Death'.

articles.title: Duct tape kept out more flood water than sandbags in laboratory tests
articles.author: Stuart McLelland, Deputy Director of the Energy and Environment Institute, University of Hull
paras: Could a cheap roll of duct tape help protect your home from flooding? New research suggests it could make a surprisingly big difference.

In controlled tests, correctly applied duct tape on the outside of a household door reduced water leakage by 97-98%. The findings suggest that a simple low-cost measure could substantially reduce the amount of water entering a home during a flood. This is important as one of the key lessons from flood resilience research is that the best time to protect a property is before floodwater arrives.

The UK government’s 2025 FloodReady Review called for practical, affordable measures that help households understand their risks and to prepare for flooding. And one potential contribution to this agenda might sound unlikely, at first glance.

Duct tape is more commonly associated with household repairs than flood protection. However, tests colleagues and I conducted at the University of Hull demonstrated how much water can enter a property through an unprotected doorway during a flood.

Inside our laboratory we tested modern wooden, uPVC and composite household doors, installed by trade professionals. We captured any water that leaked through the door in a sealed enclosure behind the door, as we increased water depth in 5cm increments to a maximum depth of 60cm. We pumped out any water that leaked through the door and continuously measured the rate of water leakage to evaluate the performance of doors and different types of protection applied to them.

When testing sandbags we stacked 54 sandbags with plastic sheeting between the door and the sandbags. For tape, the same person applied the tape for all tests to minimise any bias. It took about 10-20 minutes to apply the tape to each door.

For unprotected doors, leakage often reached thousands of litres per hour at 60cm water depth. Applying duct tape across the external door reduced that leakage by 97-98%. Specialist sealing tapes achieved even greater reductions.

For decades, sandbags have been portrayed as the go-to emergency response to flooding. But sandbags have practical limitations. They are heavy to transport, labour-intensive to deploy and difficult to dispose of after contact with contaminated floodwater. And of course people don’t keep a supply of sandbags ready to deploy.

In our tests, sandbags provided less effective protection against leakage through tested doorways compared to the tape-based sealing methods. Their performance varied with water depth and at their most effective only reduced leakage by 70% compared to an unprotected door at the same water depth.

The cost difference is striking. A household may already have duct tape or be able to purchase a roll for £10 or less, while finding and deploying sandbags involves significant additional costs, transport and effort.

Duct tape is not a substitute for professionally designed flood doors, barriers or a property-specific flood resilience plan. It is a temporary measure that may reduce water entering through particular gaps; it cannot guarantee a dry home or prevent water entering through other routes, including walls, floors, and drains.

Its effectiveness will depend on the condition of the door and frame, the surfaces to which the tape is applied, the quality of the seal and flood conditions. For properties at significant flood risk, professionally assessed protection remains important. For others, low-cost temporary measures could provide an additional layer of protection, though they cannot guarantee a property will remain dry.

Resilient households think ahead. They know whether they are at risk, sign up for flood warnings and have a plan for protecting valuables, moving vehicles and shutting off utilities if necessary. Adding duct tape to an emergency flood kit can be another small step in that process.

The wider lesson is that flood resilience does not have to start with a major investment. A £10 roll of duct tape cannot stop a flood. But our research suggests it could help keep out some of the water entering through a doorway. And that makes it a useful part of a wider plan to be prepared before the water arrives.

Stuart McLelland receives funding from Flood Re who funded this study. Stuart McLelland is a member of the PFR Roundtable, the DEFRA PFR Technical Group and the Flood Performance Certificate Oversight Group.

articles.title: Could your plastic film packaging serve a purpose? We won’t know until recycling laws change
articles.author: Robert Hargreaves, Lecturer in Law, York St John University
paras: From the clear covering on your microwave meal to the flimsy bread bag lying on the kitchen counter, plastic film is notoriously tricky to recycle. But what if those annoying bits of plastic waste could be put to better use?
This hard-to-reycle plastic could be transformed, potentially into a source of fuel, but the UK’s current recycling rules make it difficult for companies to innovate and experiment.

The main legal barrier is the definition of recycling itself. Under the rules UK waste law is built on, recycling cannot include turning waste into anything that will be used as fuel. A separate category for the plastics that are the hardest to recycle, recognising fuel made from waste that would otherwise be burned, would give companies more scope to experiment with new ways to process it.

As a legal researcher, I study how the law decides what counts as recycling. My work raises a simple question. If the rules allowed it, could dealing with one problem, plastic waste, also help ease another, our dependence on imported fuel?

In Darlington in north-east England, a chemical recycling company has received planning permission for what it describes as the UK’s first large-scale plant for recycling plastic film. The company, Endolys, plans to take up to 120,000 tonnes a year of waste plastic film, such as bread bags, wrappers and pouches, and turn it into so-called pyrolysis oil, subject to an environmental permit from the Environment Agency being granted.

Pyrolysis involves heating plastic to a very high temperature without air. With no oxygen, the plastic cannot burn, so it breaks down into pyrolysis oil along with some gas and solid residue. It is a little like making charcoal, where wood is heated without being allowed to catch fire.

Recycling waste plastic film in this way has had mixed results around the world. In Texas, US, ExxonMobil now processes more than 70,000 tonnes of plastic waste a year this way. But in the Netherlands, a Rotterdam pyrolysis plant with a deal to supply Shell never reached its planned capacity and has now closed for good. In Japan, a plant using a related process with very hot, pressurised water opened in 2025, and can process 20,000 tonnes of waste plastic a year.

What happens to the oil? Plastic doesn’t go in one end and come out as diesel. Pyrolysis oil is closer to crude oil. It has to be cleaned and refined before it can become fuel, or it can be used to make new plastics. The new facility at Darlington expects to produce around 80,000 tonnes of pyrolysis oil a year.
There is a catch for energy security. Endolys has agreed to sell all of that oil to a global trader for European refineries. A plant only strengthens the UK’s own supply if the oil stays in the UK.

At the moment, most of this kind of plastic is burned in incinerators. Burning plastic can produce dioxins, toxic chemicals linked to cancer, although modern incinerators filter out most of them, and must meet strict limits.

Because pyrolysis works without air, fewer of these chemicals should form. An Italian study comparing the two found the health risks from pyrolysis were low. For people living near an incinerator for many years, it put the cancer risk close to one extra case in every million people, the level the researchers treated as acceptable and a common benchmark in health risk assessments.

A German study found that turning plastic into oil rather than burning it could cut the greenhouse gas emissions from dealing with the waste by more than half, and by up to 94% as Germany’s electricity becomes cleaner.

Pyrolysis plants often burn some of their own gas to keep running, and that part is regulated much like an incinerator. Inks, food residue and chlorine from some plastics can end up in the oil and need removing. When the oil is finally burned as fuel, its pollution and carbon are released then. And in Darlington, some residents have petitioned against the plant over health fears.
UK waste policy tries to keep plastic in use as plastic, recycled into new bottles, trays and packaging. Turning plastic into fuel generally doesn’t count as recycling.

That makes sense for plastic that can be recycled. But plastic film is one of the hardest materials to deal with. Councils in England were due to start collecting it from every home by March 2027, but the government has pushed that back to 2030, partly because there aren’t yet enough places to recycle it. Meanwhile, much of it is burned to generate a little electricity.

For those genuinely leftover plastics, I believe that the line between recycling and fuel deserves a second look. At the moment, the rules do little to encourage plants like Darlington to sell their oil in the UK, so the energy security benefit goes elsewhere. Rules that rewarded keeping this oil at home could change that.

Plastic waste will never replace imported oil. On its own, Darlington’s 80,000 tonnes of oil a year would match only about 0.1% of the 61 million tonnes of oil products the UK used in 2025. That’s roughly half a day’s worth. But Darlington is one plant.

England’s rubbish still contains around 4.2 million tonnes of plastic a year. If half of that were turned into oil at Darlington’s rate and kept in the UK, it could meet a little over 2% of the country’s oil needs. With the right rules, a small, steady supply from bread bags and food wrappers in our bins could help the UK be a little less exposed to future fuel shocks.

articles.title: Is the world pricing the risk of a US diesel export ban?
articles.author: Michel Robe, Professor of Finance and Distinguished Chair, University of Richmond
paras: A spike in diesel prices is hammering broad sectors of the U.S. economy – especially agriculture and shipping – and becoming a flash point ahead of the November 2026 midterm elections.

This squeeze has prompted Republicans from hard-hit farm states to call for a ban on U.S. diesel exports, with President Donald Trump reportedly weighing the idea as well. He also announced a deal on Oct. 9 to supply Russian diesel to U.S. and global markets.
Meanwhile, the G7 countries have agreed to release an additional 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from their emergency reserves.

What would happen if the U.S. did enact an export ban? It’s a net exporter of petroleum products, so such a move would split the U.S. and world markets for diesel. The resulting mismatch between domestic demand and supply could depress U.S. diesel prices in the short term.

This would give some relief to American consumers, at least temporarily. But as a professor of finance who studies commodities and market volatility, I also see a big adverse shock hitting the rest of the world under that scenario.

The current political response to pricey diesel, however, shouldn’t be a surprise. A recent paper of mine, co-authored with two other economists, asks more broadly when governments are more inclined to restrict commodity exports. We found that export bans are more likely when prices are high and when politicians start weighing the preferences of commodity users, like consumers, over those of commodity producers, like the oil industry.
This could be what’s happening right now, amid record energy prices and just a few weeks from Election Day.

Diesel prices are hovering near all-time highs. The Energy Information Administration reports that the average price of the U.S. benchmark, known as ultra-low sulfur diesel, has topped US$7 per gallon in some regions like the West Coast.

Soaring energy prices are also continuing to push U.S. inflation up more broadly. Consumer prices in September jumped year-on-year by a higher-than-expected 3.7%, with gas prices responsible for more than half of the most recent monthly increase.

How did this happen? Before the conflict with Iran erupted in February 2026, key diesel exporters included Russia, Middle Eastern producers, the United States and China. Since then, those first two export sources have withered.

Russia, now in the fifth year of its war against Ukraine, banned diesel exports in July 2026 after Ukraine launched an effective air campaign that has knocked out more than half of Russia’s oil refinery capacity and destroyed many diesel storage-tank farms. That retaliatory campaign has pushed Russia from being a top diesel exporter to importing refined oil products, including diesel.

Meanwhile, in the Middle East, crude oil prices surged following missile attacks against Iran at the end of February. The Strait of Hormuz, which was the transit route for more than one-fifth of the global crude oil and natural gas output, essentially shut down amid fears over Iran targeting commercial ships sailing through.

Since then, increased shipments through Saudi and Emirati pipelines and actions by the U.S. Navy in the strait have helped restart petroleum flows. But the threat to Hormuz shipping remains real, as seen by recent strikes by Iranian forces on multiple tankers in early October.

These shocks have changed the economics of petroleum shipments in two ways. First, the price of transporting oil has more than quintupled, as tanker owners charge record fees to travel through the strait. Those fees, of course, bleed into the price that diesel buyers pay.

Second, in the strait, the content of tanker cargo has changed. Many ships are now loaded with crude oil, rather than diesel, after Iranian strikes on Gulf countries earlier this year knocked out a substantial share of the Middle Eastern refining capacity. Insofar as there isn’t much additional refinery capacity elsewhere in the world, even these restored crude oil flows can’t bring diesel prices down to prewar levels.
What an export ban would look like

The effects of removing Russian and Middle Eastern diesel from the market are being felt worldwide. One result is that U.S. diesel exports to the rest of the world have surged due to heightened foreign demand for the product and the high prices it can fetch abroad. Those export flows have been accompanied by the diesel price spike at home.

That jump in domestic prices is what’s driving discussions of a possible ban on U.S. diesel exports, and it reflects a dynamic that my co-authors and I laid out in our study of commodity export restrictions and bans. While we focused on agricultural markets, our findings also apply to the current diesel crunch.

Governments of commodity-exporting countries typically balance the interests of commodity producers and exporters, who prefer high prices, against those of domestic consumers, who like lower prices. When consumers’ wishes matter relatively more – for example, as elections approach – the likelihood of a ban rises.

American consumers never like high energy prices. Nowadays, after years of elevated inflation, they seem especially unhappy about them. Until the Iran war, Trump had been able to tout a substantial fall in petroleum product prices after he returned to office in January 2025. That’s no longer the case.

Higher diesel prices are being felt across the economy. The fuel is used to heat homes, especially in the Northeast, and to power machinery, tractors, trucks, boats and trains. This is why farmers and transportation operators are especially hard hit. Furthermore, these businesses typically try to pass their cost increases on to their customers. So shoppers are shelling out more for groceries and any other goods that must be transported.
Under the scenario of an export ban, the cost of U.S. diesel might fall in the short run, but world prices would spike. Soaring prices, however, would not be the only issue for the rest of the world.

Our research shows that a major exporting country’s ban would also increase market uncertainty and volatility. This is because restricting exports would effectively concentrate the rest of the world’s production, making the remaining supply base more fragile and increasing the rest of the world’s exposure to any subsequent output shocks.

If other countries think that their diesel situation is already bad, it would be much worse under a U.S. export ban. And the G7 move to release more diesel into the global market indicates that the rest of the world might understand how U.S. politics could lead to that outcome.

articles.title: Can the Greens stick to their democratic principles?
articles.author: Mitya Pearson, Associate Professor, University of Warwick
paras: The Green Party of England and Wales’ prospects have fluctuated dramatically in recent years. At times, it has appeared on the cusp of becoming a major force at Westminster.
During this period, the Greens have had to balance their belief in internal party democracy while operating in a modern media and electoral environment.

Around the 2015 general election, the party’s membership and broader popularity surged, before the Labour Party picked Jeremy Corbyn as its leader and its subsequent move to the left stalled much of the Greens’ momentum.

Keir Starmer’s time as Labour leader allowed the Greens to once again successfully court progressive voters. They gained a record four MPs at the 2024 election, and their poll rating grew after Zack Polanski became leader in 2025.

But their popularity has slumped once again recently, something seemingly confirmed by their second-place finish in the recent Holborn and St Pancras byelection. They did, though, register their second-highest vote share in a byelection.

Over this period the Green Party of England and Wales and its sister parties in the rest of the UK have managed to consistently gain political representation at various levels, even if the Greens’ popularity and prominence have oscillated.
Dilution of democratic principles

Green parties are strongly associated with internal democracy. Many green parties have therefore had to manage this commitment once they have achieved national prominence and electoral success, at times leading to some dilution of democratic principles in the name of professionalisation. This was implied by Michels’ idea of the “iron law of oligarchy”: political parties tend towards hierarchical structures in the name of efficiency.

The Green Party of England and Wales is a pretty typical case. Historically, it had a strong, early commitment to the idea that it would not just seek to implement policies different from those of other parties, but approach politics in a distinct manner, including through participatory and democratic decision-making processes. There were numerous arguments over this within the Greens, reflecting the “fundi-realo” divide seen in Green parties in other countries.

In the early 1990s there were factious disputes over the “Green 2000” proposals for a more centralised organisational structure, with the reforms ultimately being adopted. Subsequently, a Rubicon was crossed in 2007 when the Greens voted to create the position of leader, replacing the previous shared principal speaker roles.

Nonetheless, the Greens have remained highly democratic compared to most other parties in the UK. Their policies are decided by votes at the party conference, which then provides the “foundation” for election manifestos and political programmes.

The Greens’ commitment to members deciding policy has created challenges for it as the party has become more prominent. At times members have voted for policies which have proved controversial, including the “Zionism is racism” motion which was recently passed at its conference. This has been widely criticised, with various Green figures distancing themselves from it.

The leader’s role is somewhat ambiguous as the party’s policy foundation is decided by conference votes and a leader may end up defending a position they may not agree with. Polanski said that he would have voted against the Zionism motion.

Journalists have often picked up on policies in areas such as migration, drugs and defence which have been agreed at Green conference, but can be awkward for party leaders to explain in media interviews. This is partly a product of the system where the party provides an underlying body of policy, but a different manifesto is put forward at elections.

The most likely route for the Greens to enter the UK government would be via a coalition. This is increasingly plausible given the British party system’s fragmentation. However, Westminster’s culture is not used to this type of arrangement and larger parties can face pressure to rule out working with controversial partners.

Indeed, Labour figures recently ruled out future cooperation with the Greens after the Zionism motion, and some Labour MPs even involved the police. Green leaders may also require their party members’ approval during any future coalition negotiations, which for most other UK party leaders would be unnecessary.

The Greens have, additionally, been grappling with practical issues. The party has grown, reaching over 200,000 members, meaning it is difficult for more than a small proportion of members to attend conferences and vote on policy.

There are reports that the current Green leadership has been looking at ways to amend its system of policymaking in light of its enlarged membership. Polanski has argued in the aftermath of the Zionism debate that “our party democracy must now evolve”. It seems very unlikely, however, that this will lead to a full-scale jettisoning of the party’s democratic structure.

Political parties’ roots and principles shape and constrain them, which means that they are often not totally free to make choices even if they consider them to be in their immediate tactical interest, and the Greens’ commitment to internal democracy runs very deep. None of the challenges which have been outlined here are necessarily insurmountable either.
Nonetheless, the Zionism motion has highlighted some of the tensions within a party, which is increasingly prominent in British politics, deciding its policy democratically.

articles.title: Cities are sinking – but citywide averages hide the real problem
articles.author: Emma Colven, Senior Lecturer in Environment and Society, King's College London
paras: Cities worldwide are sinking at alarming rates, but that doesn’t mean the ground is sinking at the same rate everywhere. Some neighbourhoods may be far more affected than others close by, with serious consequences for their residents.

Land subsidence – the gradual sinking of the ground surface – is a global urban problem. Rapid development often drives excessive groundwater extraction, which can cause underground sediments to compact and the land above to sink. The risk of flooding is exacerbated by rising sea levels and more intense rainfall associated with climate change.
One recent study estimated that about 71% of the global coastal population lives in subsiding regions, many of which are densely populated and already threatened by sea-level rise.

Advances in satellite monitoring now allow researchers to measure subsidence across cities at fine spatial scales. In a new study in Nature Cities a team of Chinese scientists used nine years of these satellite images to assess 465 large cities worldwide. They found cities in Asia are subsiding fastest, and that cities in developing countries are generally sinking faster than those in wealthier countries.
But citywide patterns can conceal big differences within individual cities, with important implications for where flood protection is most needed.
Jakarta – among the world’s fastest sinking cities

We have become very aware of this in our own research in the Indonesian capital Jakarta. Now the world’s most populous city, Jakarta has for many years been the poster child for sinking cities. Significant areas already lie below sea level and continued subsidence could put more of the city below it. Some areas in Jakarta are sinking more rapidly than others: the city’s northern coastal area, for instance, sinks up to 7cm a year according to our model for 2016-24.

As a low-lying delta city in the tropics, crossed by 13 rivers, Jakarta is already vulnerable to floods from both rivers and tides. Land subsidence makes these floods more frequent and severe. In coastal northern areas such as Muara Angke, where informal settlements are common, flooding can occur every other day. This affects some of the city’s most vulnerable communities.
Land subsidence is a planning problem

To protect the city, Jakarta has constructed a network of seawalls, water gates, polder systems, dykes, and pumping stations. Something similar is needed in many other subsiding coastal cities on Java, the world’s most populated island, and there are now plans to construct a giant sea wall across much of northern Java.
Yet flood defences alone won’t be able to cope and protect Jakarta or other Javanese cities from flooding without changes to the overall planning system.

Land subsidence had not been fully integrated into Jakarta’s flood management planning until recently. Groundwater extraction regulations were introduced in 2021 and implemented in 2023, despite land subsidence being discussed for more than three decades.

A core problem remains the lack of a reliable piped water supply, making it desirable for residential and large commercial buildings to extract their own groundwater. Enforcement has improved but remains challenging: groundwater is notoriously difficult to manage as it is a hidden or “fugitive” resource.

Fortunately, land subsidence from excessive groundwater extraction can be reversed. When groundwater is replenished, the land surface may rise again. That being said, even immediately stopping groundwater extraction would not halt sinking abruptly.
Long-term adaptive management is urgently needed, supported by a comprehensive policy framework that combines groundwater regulation, extraction control, and overall water supply management.

Injecting water into the ground to replenish the aquifer has proven effective in managing subsidence in places such as Las Vegas and Shanghai. But the same approach is not straightforward in Jakarta, where land subsidence is driven by a combination of factors, including water loss deep below ground. Addressing this is technically complex and expensive, making regulation and piped water essential to tackling the problem.

Subsidence may be a global problem, but it is driven by locally specific factors and can only be addressed with an understanding of local patterns. This is because the causes and impacts of land subsidence are shaped by urban development, water management, and all the other policies and decisions in the making of the city.

As cities worldwide continue to sink, we need to continually examine these changes at the local scale. Averages across a whole city can tell us how big the problem is, but knowing where the land is sinking fastest – and who lives there – is essential to deciding how best to respond.

articles.title: Five types of disinformation – and how to spot red flags that trigger climate inaction
articles.author: Mark Maslin, Professor of Earth System Science, UCL
paras: We’re living in an age of constant information: tweets, headlines, reels, reports. It’s everywhere, all the time. But here’s the challenge: not all of it is true. Some of it is intentionally misleading. A lot is AI-generated. From outright climate denial to more subtle greenwashing, disinformation is not just a digital nuisance – it’s a real threat.
Disinformation is false, fabricated or manipulated information that intends to deceive, while misinformation is false or misleading information shared without the intent to deceive.

AI is playing an increasingly powerful role in how information and disinformation spread. AI bots are software programmes designed to simulate human behaviour online. They can generate content, post on social media, chat with users and operate at massive scale. AI tools can create realistic-looking fake articles, images, even deepfakes of experts. Bots can amplify these messages to manipulate public opinion – especially during key moments such as elections or climate summits.

Michael Mann, a professor at the University of Pennsylvania, has broken down climate disinformation into five key groups. Here’s how to spot those five forms of disinformation and counter them with scientific evidence.

Minimising the seriousness of the climate crisis involves classic comments such as “it’s not that bad” or “climate change is natural – it’s always happened”. Downplaying creates complacency. It dulls public urgency, delays policy action and makes the problem seem less immediate than it is.

But science shows that this has been the warmest decade on record and global temperatures will continue to increase every year due to greenhouse gas emissions. In 2025 there were 157 incidences of extreme weather around the world with significant consequences for more than 100 million people.

This type of disinformation acknowledges climate change as real but argues that action can wait. Comments include “we should wait until the technology is better”, “let’s not rush into drastic policies”, “innovation will solve this – eventually” or “we need more research before acting”.
Delay equals denial in slow motion. It gives the illusion of concern while justifying inaction, letting emissions continue and narrowing the window for meaningful action.

It also means that the public and politicians ignore the urgency of climate change and are not preparing. For example, many countries, including the UK, are not even planning to adapt to the changes that are already occurring – such as sea level rise, more frequent heatwaves, drought, wildfires, floods and storms.

Deflection shifts attention away from systemic solutions and toward other issues, often to avoid responsibility or blame someone else. You might hear people say things like “individuals need to do more – stop blaming companies”, “until big polluters act, nothing we do matters”, “aren’t there more urgent problems to focus on?” or even “what about China?”.
Deflection diverts energy from collective action and structural change. It stalls progress and divides public support.

The science clearly shows that the world must decarbonise the entire economy and reach a point by 2050 at which no additional greenhouse gases enter the atmosphere. So every country and every company has to change – and as quickly as possible.

Division aims to create distrust and polarise the conversation. This turns climate action into a political or cultural wedge. You might hear phrases like “climate change is just a leftist agenda”, “scientists are part of a global conspiracy”, “they want to take away your freedom in the name of climate”, “net zero will make your energy prices go up” and the classic “they’re just trying to control you”.

Division undermines trust in science, institutions and each other. It fuels tribalism, making cooperation harder when it’s needed most. The fossil fuel industry and lobby invented and used the carbon footprint approach to blame individual consumption instead of admitting that the problem is about the global supply of energy.
The latest approach involves blaming climate scientists for not communicating effectively and not making the public and politicians aware of the true risks.

Doomism promotes the idea that the climate crisis is already beyond saving, leading to apathy instead of action. You might hear comments such as “we’re past the tipping point — it’s hopeless”, “the planet is doomed no matter what we do”, “why bother trying?” and “it’s too late – nothing we do matters”.
Doomism paralyses people with despair, just as much as denial. It discourages solutions, undermines collective action, and hands victory to the status quo.

Yet there are so many positive solutions that exist which not only reduce greenhouse gas emissions but also make peoples lives better. A global switch to renewable energy creates local energy security, reduces energy costs and reduces harmful air pollution generated by burning fossil fuels.
Getting people to switch to more plant-based diets makes everyone more healthy, reduces healthcare costs and reduces deforestation.
Encouraging critical thinking is a powerful antidote to disinformation. Certain red flags can help you spot disinformation that might be misleading or wrong.
If a post is designed to provoke outrage or fear, take a moment before reacting. Emotion is often used to bypass critical thinking.
Messages that pressure you to “share now” or “spread this before it’s deleted” are classic manipulation tactics.

Does an article cite reliable data or expert opinion? If there aren’t any credible sources, avoid amplifying it. And if there’s no transparency about the source, proceed with caution and be wary of anonymous authors.
If you spot even one of these signs, pause, verify and think before you share.

This article was inspired by the Climate Change Disinformation talk given by Shooka Bidarian at EarthFest and the five categories defined by Prof. Michael Mann (University of Pennsylvania).
