articles.title: How Trump’s disaster aid delays and FEMA cuts could galvanize the ‘movable middle’ in the 2026 elections
articles.author: Dana R. Fisher, Director of the Center for Environment, Community & Equity and Professor in the School of International Service, American University School of International Service
paras: When Hurricane Isaias hit the Florida Panhandle on Oct. 9, 2026, it was just the latest weather disaster for Americans in a year that continues to break records.

The hottest U.S. summer on record left millions of Americans facing life-threatening heat waves. Extreme heat and drought set the stage for wildfires. Flooding from powerful storms and days of heavy rainfall inundated communities in several states. And now a “Super El Niño,” on top of already rising temperatures and sea levels, is expected to make extreme events worse, at least into spring 2027.

In the past, states relied heavily on federal aid and expertise to respond quickly to disasters. But in communities across the U.S., people recovering from floods, storms and wildfires in 2025 and 2026 have been left waiting much longer for federal aid – if it arrives at all.
Will there be political consequences in the midterm elections for the slow aid and lack of government assistance?

The answer to that question runs through the ways the Trump administration has changed disaster response and federal disaster aid. As a professor who has written for years about civic engagement and climate policy, I have reason to believe that voters’ frustration with slow disaster aid may show up at the polls.
Cuts to FEMA hobbled federal disaster help
Even though the United States is experiencing more disasters as the climate changes, the federal programs meant to help Americans recover are being diminished.

The Federal Emergency Management Agency has faced significant cuts to funding and staff since the Trump administration took office in January 2025. The administration initially talked about abolishing the agency, arguing that states and communities could deal with disasters on their own. It created a plan to cut FEMA’s staffing by 50%, but in September 2026, a judge found that plan to be unlawful.

FEMA lost over 17% of its trained staff members in 2025 alone, including hundreds of people who were on call to respond to disasters. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin continues to defend the administration’s goal of a leaner workforce at the agency.

The Trump administration also withheld billions of dollars meant to help states reduce their disaster risk and protect homes, hospitals and other structures from storm damage. Lawsuits forced the administration to restore some of the funds, but many communities are still struggling on their own.
These changes have tangible effects on how well states are able to recover from disasters and how well they can prepare for the disaster risks ahead as the climate changes.
Slower aid, if it arrives at all
The Trump administration is also taking longer to approve emergency funding after disasters than past administrations did and denying more of those requests.
In 2025 it denied 26% of requests for major disaster declarations, which unlock immediate federal aid. That was up from an average of 15% over the previous two decades.

An independent analysis of FEMA data exposes some clear patterns in funding delays under the Trump administration. The review found that major disaster declarations have taken an average of nearly 10 weeks to be issued during the current Trump administration, up from an average of three weeks or less over the previous two decades.

The administration says it is simply conducting more thorough reviews when governors make these aid requests. But people caught in disasters don’t have time to wait. Major disaster aid includes individual assistance, such as temporary housing, loans and repair grants, that disaster survivors need quickly to recover.

The review also found that about 85% of the requests for federal assistance from states that went for Donald Trump in the 2024 election were eventually approved, while only about half of requests have been approved in states that voted for his Democratic opponent, Kamala Harris.

A separate Associated Press report in July 2026 noted that no other president had such a sharp partisan divide in approving disaster declaration requests between Republican and Democratic governors since at least 1989, when a federal law set rules for disaster determinations.
Disaster failures can mobilize political moderates
A handful of studies, including mine, have found that people who have experienced a disaster often have higher levels of civic engagement.

In my study, civic engagement included contacting elected officials, signing petitions, attending public meetings, participating in boycotts or joining protests, among other actions. We didn’t look at the connection to voting patterns, but I believe there is good reason to expect our findings to extend to voting as well.

The relationship between experiencing a disaster and level of civic engagement was strongest for political moderates who are sometimes referred to as the “movable middle” – they could swing in either political direction if they have reason to do so.

Given the disasters America has seen in recent years and the sharp drop in federal assistance, I expect that political moderates who become more civically engaged will play a significant role in the midterm elections this year.
How FEMA cuts play out in a crisis
Several recent disasters have shown what happens when the federal government isn’t prepared to respond quickly.

After the devastating July 4 floods that swept through Texas Hill Country in 2025, the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees FEMA, waited three days before approving funding to send federal search-and-rescue teams, a Congressional report confirmed. Other funding approvals took an average of 12 days, leaving local and state programs to fill critical gaps in disaster systems.
In summer 2026, Texas was hit with floods again. The president approved assistance for some of the counties after a seven-week delay. Other requests for assistance were still waiting months later.
FEMA denied individual and statewide assistance to Michigan after severe storms and tornadoes tore up homes across several rural communities in March 2026.

With highly contested Senate races looming in both states, these actions by the Trump administration could color voters’ views or contribute to a lack of enthusiasm for the party in power and even increase support for the opposition.

A survey conducted by Pew Research Center in May 2025 found that the majority of Americans believe that it is a good idea for the federal government to provide financial assistance to help people rebuild after disasters in place at high risk of extreme weather.

These findings are relatively consistent across political parties: 60% of those who identified as Republican or leaning Republican said they believed it was a good idea, as did 68% of those who identified as Democrat or leaning Democrat.

Trump recently started announcing disaster aid approvals in states consequential to the control of Congress in the midterm elections, including in Wisconsin and Ohio. In some cases, he coupled his candidate endorsements with disaster funding announcements.
I don’t believe those late announcements will move the needle in his party’s favor at this late date.

articles.title: What an ancient volcanic eruption teaches us about resilience today
articles.author: Peter Jordan, Professor of Archaeology, Lund University
paras: When a massive environmental disaster strikes, do societies simply collapse and disappear? Or do people find a way to adapt, rebuild and recover?
As a researcher studying ancient societies and their environments, these aren’t just academic questions to me – they can also offer useful perspectives on our own climate-threatened future.

To understand how human communities handle cataclysmic shocks, my colleagues and I looked back 7,300 years. We investigated what happened to the prehistoric Jōmon hunter-gatherer populations after they were hit by the Kikai-Akahoya eruption in Japan – the largest volcanic eruption since the end of the last ice age.

This enormous underwater volcanic eruption was utterly devastating, blasting out of the seabed without warning, battering the Japanese islands with powerful earthquakes and massive tsunamis. The eruption pumped volcanic ash high up into the atmosphere which then rained down and blanketed the landscape in metre-deep layers of toxic dust.

This volcanic ash choked coastlines, destroyed inland rivers and killed off lush forests for decades. Near the epicentre of the eruption, the environmental destruction lasted for centuries, utterly destroying local food systems. For the Jōmon hunter-gather people who relied on harvesting natural resources in the wild, this had catastrophic and enduring shocks on their food security.

For a long time, archaeologists have debated what happened to communities during the aftermath. Some have argued that it led to a total apocalypse where all human life abruptly ended. Others have insisted on total continuity, suggesting people just pushed through.

Our new research moves past this rigid, binary debate. By tracking population levels across different regions of Japan before and after the blast, we uncovered a much more complex and fascinating story.

We initially assumed that thicker ash meant higher population declines. The data partially backed this up, showing major loss of life near the eruption. But our research has revealed some real surprises.

Forager populations closest to the epicentre were actually already declining before the volcano ever blew. So the disaster compounded preexisting vulnerabilities among these small groups of people who survived by moving around a lot to gather sufficient resources, such as plants, nuts and wild game.

In contrast, population levels actually boomed after the eruption in certain areas quite close to the destruction. Survivors didn’t just sit there and perish; they migrated away from the worst-hit zones into safer regions.

Inland survivors quickly moved to coastal areas where marine ecosystems recovered faster, shifting their entire economy to survive. The Jōmon people appear to have reacted and also adapted quite rapidly.

Paradoxically, populations living far away from the volcano (where people should have been safe) stagnated or declined after the eruption. This was probably due to a volcanic winter, where ash clouds blocked the sunlight, reducing plant growth and also animal numbers on which the Jōmon hunter-gatherers relied on for their main food supplies.
What do these prehistoric responses mean for us today?

The core insight of our research is the vital role of human agency. True resilience isn’t about perfectly maintaining the status quo or seamlessly continuing as if nothing happened. Rather than causing total collapse, this ancient disaster triggered a complex mix of migration, adaptation and recovery.
Survivors chose to move. They forged entirely new social networks, innovated new economies, and found creative, resourceful ways to thrive in a permanently altered world.

By studying these ancient disasters, we generate a more dynamic vision for modern resilience. Survival is not a fixed state. The lessons of the Jōmon people remind us that our future in the face of climate shocks and other disasters won’t only be decided by environmental conditions, but also by our collective social actions and capacity for making decisions.

articles.title: A record-breaking El Niño is still developing – likely bringing a cold winter to the UK
articles.author: Chloe Brimicombe, Postdoctoral Researcher, Climate Science, University of Oxford
paras: The UK could be in for a wet and stormy autumn followed by a colder, calmer winter – and an unusually powerful El Niño may be partly responsible.

El Niño is a natural climate pattern in the tropical Pacific, but its effects can be felt around the world. This year’s event is already the strongest on record, and is expected to strengthen further before peaking later this year.

El Niño is the warm phase of the El Niño Southern Oscillation, a natural cycle involving the tropical Pacific Ocean and the atmosphere. During El Niño, unusually warm sea-surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific reverse the direction of certain winds, affecting weather patterns far beyond the region. A stronger El Niño has a larger influence on global weather patterns than a weaker one.
So how does a climate pattern thousands of miles away affect the weather in the UK and Europe?
How El Niño reaches Britain

The link between El Niño and weather in the UK is complicated and not direct. Weather systems in different parts of the world can influence one another through links known as teleconnections. El Niño has teleconnections both in the troposphere, the part of the atmosphere we live in, and the stratosphere, the part of the atmosphere just above us.

Through these teleconnections, El Niño is linked to the North Atlantic oscillation, a weather pattern which involves differences in air pressure over the ocean. El Niño is associated with the oscillation’s negative phase, when this pressure difference is less than usual. This tends to weaken the winds that bring mild air from the Atlantic to the UK, increasing the chance of colder, calmer weather in late winter.

El Niño can also affect the stratospheric polar vortex, a band of strong winds that circles the Earth high above the Arctic. It has been found to weaken the vortex which then can disrupt the jet stream – the high moving body of air that is a driver behind much of the UK’s weather. This can increase the chances of storms and wetter and potentially colder weather in the autumn and early winter.

Vortex weakening is also linked with an increase in sudden stratospheric warming events, when parts of the atmospheric layer above ours warm up rapidly. These events are one driver of some cold snaps in the UK as they can alter the jet stream and allow colder air to reach the country. However, not all of these events result in cold weather in the UK.

These links are relevant to the UK’s latest seasonal forecasting from the Met Office. This forecast shows autumn is likely to bring wetter and stormier weather followed by colder, calmer weather in winter.

Colder, calmer weather in UK winters is known to present a challenge for energy production from renewable sources, especially when it is also cloudy. Wind power generates 40% or more of the UK’s electricity during winter, and cold, calm periods can require more gas power to make up for lower wind generation and increased demand for heating.

El Niño also improves our ability to [predict weather at long lead times] because of its links with major drivers of different weather patterns. This includes for winter weather but also in some cases summer heatwaves. There are limits, however: we cannot tell when a particular heatwave or storm will occur. We cannot predict the associated impacts in detail. We can only say whether a certain season is more likely to be hotter or drier or colder or wetter, and identify related trends in impacts.
It is important to remember that two things happening at the same time do not mean they cause one another. In the case of El Niño and the weather in the UK, the response is non-linear and not direct.

There is little evidence yet about whether human-induced climate change is causing more intense or more frequent El Niños. But it certainly amplifies the warming effect of climate change. Some research suggests that it can also amplify climate whiplash, where some regions flipflop from wet weather to hot-dry weather either within seasons or in one season after another.
Chloe Brimicombe receives funding from the Economic and Social Sciences Research Council (ESRC) and she is a heat ambassador for Shade the UK.

articles.title: Councils that restrict harmful advertising won’t lose out on profits
articles.author: Kate Whitman, Research Fellow, University of Portsmouth
paras: For cash-strapped councils, turning away much-needed income by restricting adverts for junk food, fossil fuels or other harmful products might seem like a policy they can ill afford.
But a new report, published by the advocacy alliance Sustain and carried out by our team at the University of Portsmouth, suggests otherwise.

Our report found no evidence that councils introducing healthier food advertising policies lost advertising revenue when compared to places without such a policy. The finding held for councils across the UK with different advertising sites (from bus shelters to benches), locations and contract arrangements.

For our analysis, we sent freedom of information requests to all local councils in the UK. From the 360 responses received, only 38 councils provided enough data on the annual percentage change of revenue (between 2019-23) to allow for comparison. Three of those 38 councils had introduced healthier food advertising policies during that five-year period; the rest (35) did not have those policies.

By comparing the revenue of local governments that implemented a healthier food advertising policy to those without, a statistical model assessed whether council revenues were now below what would have been expected had they not implemented a healthier foods advertising policy. The findings show that councils did not lose potential revenue from implementing this policy.

Concern about lost income has been one of the practical arguments made against stronger advertising policies. Yet restricting harmful products does not mean leaving billboards and bus shelters empty. Advertising space can instead be filled by more socially beneficial campaigns, such as healthy products, while companies affected by the rules can switch to promoting products that comply with them.

This can also reduce the financial pressure on other public services. Transport for London’s restrictions on advertising foods high in fat, salt and sugar have been associated with households purchasing around 1,000 fewer calories from unhealthy foods each week. Modelling of the policy estimated that resulting health benefits could save the NHS and social care system £218 million over the lifetime of the current population.
Now councils are beginning to apply the same thinking beyond junk food.

Public bodies are extending the principle already applied to tobacco, alcohol and unhealthy food to fossil fuels and other high-carbon products: that publicly controlled advertising space should not be used to promote forms of consumption that undermine public health or environmental goals.

More than a dozen UK councils including Sheffield and Edinburgh have adopted some form of restriction on high-carbon advertising, covering products and services such as fossil fuels, flights and non-electric cars.
And the boundaries continue to expand.

Bristol City Council recently became the first UK council to restrict advertising for ultra-fast fashion (brands that launch new designs on a daily or weekly not seasonal basis, leading to accelerated overproduction and waste) on council-owned sites, alongside new curbs on promoting fossil fuels, SUVs, airlines and cruises. The move brings an industry associated with high levels of production, consumption and waste within the scope of councils’ environmental advertising policies.

In another UK first, Portsmouth City Council included single-use plastics in its list of restricted products, alongside fossil fuels, non-electric cars and unhealthy food. Their inclusion signals a recognition of the environmental costs of disposable plastic packaging – and that an advert for a product packaged in single-use plastic is, in effect, an advert for both.

These decisions point towards a change in thinking. By expanding policies to include ultra-fast fashion and single-use plastics, UK councils appear to be recognising a wider range of environmental harms associated with the products advertised in public spaces, from the resources used to produce them to the waste they leave behind.
It also raises a broader question about whether council-owned advertising space should encourage forms of consumption that conflict with councils’ own commitments on public health, climate and waste.

However, developments outside the UK suggest this approach could go further. In May, Amsterdam became the first capital city to introduce legally binding restrictions on public advertising for fossil-fuel products and services. Those include flights, cruises and petrol and diesel cars, as well as meat. The inclusion of meat extends restrictions beyond products directly associated with fossil fuels to another major source of consumption-related environmental impacts.

The question for UK councils, then, is not simply whether these policies work, but how much further they are prepared to go. Until now, the prospect of losing advertising income has provided an economic argument for caution. Our new research weakens that argument.

If local authorities can set stronger standards without sacrificing advertising revenue, they have more room to align their advertising estates with the public health and environmental goals they are already spending money to achieve.

The shifts in both Bristol and Portsmouth show that the boundaries of acceptable advertising are already shifting in the UK. The evidence from our new report suggests councils may be able to afford to be bolder about where those boundaries are drawn.
Kate Whitman was a research consultant to Sustain for this project.

articles.title: Americans are stressed about grocery prices, so why do they toss or overlook so much ‘misfit’ food?
articles.author: Jintao Zhang, Assistant Professor of Marketing, Binghamton University, State University of New York
paras: There’s a paradox that drives the shopping decisions of many Americans: Almost three-quarters say they’re feeling stressed out about skyrocketing grocery bills. But they keep discarding large quantities of food that’s safe to eat, from crooked carrots to surplus yogurt to “best before” items pulled from shelves early.

Overall, the U.S. government estimates that 30% to 40% of all food – from consumers, retailers and producers – is thrown out. That’s not just a massive missed opportunity for people experiencing food insecurity, but it’s also a significant contribution to global warming. According to the United Nations, 8%-10% of carbon emissions globally result from food waste.

In recent years, however, a market to rescue discarded groceries and repurpose food scraps and by-products has grown dramatically. This ranges from marketing “ugly” produce to appeal to more consumers to upcycling food by-products.

I study how consumers evaluate product value and quality, and my research suggests that American shoppers are much less fixated on prices or environmental impact. Instead, they care about quality. Even when perfectly good “misfit” produce is deeply discounted, for example, many shoppers assume that the low price reflects poor quality and either walk away or reach for a fruit or vegetable they think looks better.

What does this mean for reducing food waste and shedding these purchasing biases? My research has found that smarter and more effective labeling can make a big difference. A discount or promise of lower carbon emissions isn’t enough by itself – people have to believe the food is good first.
Making ‘ugly’ food attractive

A whole retail sector is now dedicated to marketing misfit food. “Ugly produce” delivery companies like Hungry Harvest and Misfits Market are rescuing and reselling food to shoppers who want to save and reduce their carbon footprint. Misfits Market alone has rescued more than 265 million pounds (about 120 million kilos) of food since 2018 and sells it at an average discount of 35%.

Another example is Too Good To Go, an app that sells “surprise” bags of surplus food at about one-third of the retail price. It estimates that it has saved more than 26 million meals, including through partnerships with more than 530 Whole Foods stores. And the app Flashfood encourages grocers to list meat, dairy and produce nearing their best-before date at around half price and directs shoppers, including those on public food assistance, to those deals.

Consumers appear to be responding. Too Good To Go users in the U.S. saved 8.1 million meals in the first seven months of 2025, a 67% jump from the year before, while Misfits Market rescued 27 million pounds of food (about 12 million kilos) in 2025, up from 23 million (about 10 million kilos) in 2019, its first full year of operation.

This market is also using smarter labeling to grow its appeal. Shoppers who believe that food appearance is important tend to judge misshapen produce as lower quality. But labeling these offerings as “ugly” actually reduces that bias because it signals that the only flaw is cosmetic. Another study found that in-store messages that raise shoppers’ self-esteem can also make a different: In field tests, a “Different Outside. Same Inside” message successfully urged people to overlook external appearance when making judgments, whether on people or food.

This sustainability push is also playing out in the processed and semi-processed foods market, where would-be waste is converted into upcycled products. Examples include flour milled from soybean pulp, snacks that leave the fruit peel on, and “bites” made from rescued bananas.

Companies that want to market these goods can get third-party certification through Upcycled Certified if they pass an audit of their supply chain. More than 600 products from over 100 brands now carry it, and sales of certified products grew 17% from 2024 to 2025.

Here, too, perceptions of quality matter. In research on consumers’ acceptance of these foods, my co-authors and I found that they made their purchase decision based largely on whether they believed the product was as good as its conventional counterpart.

But in this case, in contrast to “ugly” produce, these products tend to be pricier, so they can’t compete through discounting. Rather, they usually sell at a premium – like this small bag of specialty flour going for $7. That means that it’s even more important they signal higher quality so they can appeal to less price-constrained shoppers.

Generational attitudes differ on this point, our research found. Gen Z, millennials and baby boomers are more willing to buy foods certified as upcycled if they agree that the quality and environmental appeal are worth it. But Gen Xers – those who were born between 1965 and 1979 – show less enthusiasm, citing a perception of lower quality.

That result fits what we generally know about Gen X shoppers. We discovered they are hard to persuade and cost-conscious, and they tend to rely much more on their own judgment. Gen Xers are also least likely to eat out or go shopping for groceries online, preferring instead to cook for themselves. That means they tend to scrutinize foods more closely in the store.
A “green” benefit won’t beat these skeptics. They need an assurance of quality from brick-and-mortar retailers they trust, rather than from online platforms.

The encouraging news from our research is that it sometimes doesn’t take much to change beliefs. In two experiments, my co-authors and I tested whether a simple logo could shift shoppers’ perceptions of foods made from rescued ingredients. We designed one version that was round, green and descriptive, following established design principles: Circular logos signal higher quality, while descriptive ones lift brand evaluations. The other was hexagonal, monochrome and bare.

We found that shoppers who saw products with the well-designed logo rated those foods higher in quality and were more willing to buy them than those who saw the same products with no logo. The poorly designed logo, meanwhile, made no difference.

It was the increase in perceived quality, in our view, that made people more willing to buy. A logo that looks credible, explains itself and signals care can change what shoppers believe. A forgettable one might as well not be there.

Closing this gap in perceptions, in short, doesn’t require shoppers to care more about the planet. It requires them to believe the food is good. The rescue economy can make that case, but it has to lead with quality and not only with conscience.

articles.title: Across the US, people don’t want data centers coming to their communities
articles.author: Neha Gour, Ph.D. Candidate in Science Communication, George Mason University
paras: Regardless of their views on politics or climate change, most Americans oppose the development of data centers in their communities.

These large buildings filled with computers that store and process digital information, increasingly to support various applications of artificial intelligence, are being built rapidly across the United States. They can bring economic investment and jobs, but the pollution created by generating the electricity they need can also harm public health, pollute air, use up water, create noise and raise energy costs.

As more data centers are proposed, some local communities are pushing back against new and prospective projects. These debates are already influencing local zoning and permitting decisions, and increasingly reaching state lawmakers.

In early September, Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey issued an executive order that no state agency will issue permits for data center development unless the project already has local approval from the municipality where it will be located. In Vermont, where Gov. Phil Scott vetoed a bill that would have imposed strict regulations on data centers, local governments are taking matters into their own hands by banning data centers in their towns.
Public opinion is playing an important role in shaping how data center expansion unfolds across the country.

We are researchers studying science communication, climate change and public health. To better understand what Americans think about these issues, we examined data from the Spring 2026 Climate Change in the American Mind survey. It is a nationally representative survey of adults in the U.S. conducted by the Yale Program on Climate Change Communication and the George Mason University Center for Climate Change Communication. Our findings align with other recent polling on the topic.
Most Americans oppose a data center in their area

In an April 2026 survey of 1,068 adults, 930 of whom are registered voters, we and our research colleagues Jennifer Carman, Seth Rosenthal, Anthony Leiserowitz and Edward Maibach asked respondents the degree to which they would support or oppose building a data center in their local area.
Just over half – 56% – said they would oppose it, while only 15% said they would support it.

The opposition is not limited to one political group. A majority of Americans in most groups across the political continuum said they oppose the development of data centers in their communities, although the extent of that opposition varies somewhat between groups.
Among registered voters, about three-quarters of liberal Democrats and about half of conservative Republicans said they oppose having a data center built in their local area.
People’s perspectives on climate change

For a closer look at how people view data centers, we built on our past work about Americans’ views about global warming and actions to reduce climate change and its effects. That research has identified six distinct groups of views on those issues, which we call “the Six Americas.”

Opposition to local data centers is highest among those in the Alarmed category, those most worried about climate change – 71% of whom opposed data centers being built in their community. But opposition is also very strong among those in the Dismissive category, who reject the idea that global warming is happening and human-caused.
These findings show that Americans with widely different beliefs about global warming can nonetheless hold similar views about local data center development.
Most Americans expect data centers to increase their electricity bills

Electricity costs are a major concern Americans have about data centers, particularly amid broader concerns about the increasing cost of living. Agreements between power companies and data center owners aren’t always clear about who will pay to generate the massive amounts of electricity involved – and it may be functionally impossible to tell if the costs are shared fairly.

A majority of Americans, 59%, expect their electricity bills to increase if a data center opens in their local area. Just 5% think their bills would decrease; 25% said they don’t know. The remaining 12% said they don’t expect their bills to be affected.
Concern about higher electricity bills is bipartisan. Among registered voters, majorities of every political group expect their bills to increase.

Electricity cost worries also span all views on climate change. The only group where a majority didn’t expect a data center to raise their power bills was the Disengaged, who don’t pay much attention to or hear about climate change very often, of whom 43% reported that expectation. But about as many of that group, 42%, said they didn’t know what might happen to their electric bills.
Most Americans support requiring data centers to offset their electricity use

We also asked Americans about one idea to address the large amount of electricity used by data centers: Instead of building new power plants to provide additional electricity, an advocacy group called Rewiring America has proposed that data center developers could be required to install rooftop solar and help weatherize and insulate nearby homes whose owners want these improvements. Those changes could generate new electricity and save additional energy to help provide the power the data center needs.
Respondents strongly supported making this idea a state or local requirement.

This proposal has considerable public support, from across the political spectrum and among the various Six Americas groups of views on climate change. Only the Dismissive group – those who dismiss the idea that climate change is happening – saw less than half of its members support these policies, even though majorities of that group oppose having a data center nearby and expect a local data center to increase their electricity bills. This is consistent with their tendency to oppose renewable energy development more generally.

The companies leading the AI boom are seeking not only computer servers, electricity and land, but also public support. As data centers continue to expand across the country, understanding Americans’ views on them, and what people expect from developers, is becoming increasingly important.
Our research shows that Americans with very different political views and opinions about global warming can share similar views about data center development.
Some state regulators and utility companies are already considering structuring electricity rates to prevent data center costs from being passed on to other customers.
At the same time, the differences matter, especially in terms of specific policies that may or may not be broadly popular.
For policymakers, data center developers and community leaders, understanding where different groups agree and disagree can help them better serve the public interest.

articles.title: How electric vehicles could help pollinators find flowers again
articles.author: James Ryalls, Senior Research Fellow in the School of Agriculture, Policy and Development, University of Reading
paras: A hidden threat is making it harder for bees, butterflies and other pollinators to do their job: air pollution is scrambling the floral scents they use to find flowers.

Colleagues and I have just published research showing that ground-level ozone and nitrogen oxides (two pollutants strongly linked to fossil fuel use) significantly impair pollinators’ ability to locate and feed from flowers.
The good news? The global shift away from fossil fuels, including the rise of electric vehicles, could eventually ease this pressure. But timing matters. Things may get worse before they get better.
Flowers release complex cocktails of volatile organic compounds, essentially their perfume, to attract pollinators. These scents act like a GPS for bees and other insects.
But when ozone and nitrogen oxides (NOx) react with these compounds, they break down or alter the chemical signals. The result is that pollinators struggle to find the flowers they need.

This isn’t just a problem for wild plants. Almonds, apples, oilseed rape, strawberries and many other important crops depend on insect pollination. When pollinators can’t forage efficiently, yields and quality can suffer.

We analysed 22 experimental studies, mostly from Europe, that tested how elevated levels of ozone and NOx affect pollinators’ ability to find and feed from flowers, as well as their overall abundance.

On average across the studies, elevated ozone reduced pollinator performance by 42%, while NOx reduced it by 46%. When the two pollutants occurred together (as they do in the real world), the average reduction was 68%.
However, only a small number of studies tested the pollutants both separately and in combination. In those comparisons, the additional impact of combining the two pollutants was relatively modest.
Pollinators’ searching efficiency – the ability to locate flowers – was hit hardest, dropping by 67% on average. Feeding efficiency and overall abundance were less affected.
This suggests the main problem with the pollution is that it disrupts pollinators’ ability to find flowers, rather than being directly toxic to the insects themselves.
The coming ozone peak – and why it happens

There is a complication, however. NOx and ground-level ozone are linked chemically, so cutting NOx emissions will not necessarily reduce ozone immediately. In fact, under a middle-of-the-road emissions scenario, global low-level ozone levels are projected to keep rising until around 2050, even as NOx emissions begin to fall.

This is partly because ozone and NOx interact in the atmosphere. NOx can react with and destroy ozone. When NOx levels are high, as they often are near roads or in cities, this “quenching” effect helps keep ozone concentrations down.

So, as we cut NOx emissions from diesel vehicles and other sources, this quenching effect weakens. With less NOx around to break it down, ozone concentrations can actually climb. Other ozone-forming pollutants, such as methane, also remain high for longer in this scenario.

Only after this mid-century peak do sustained reductions in NOx and other precursors drive ozone levels down again. Under this middle-of-the-road scenario, ozone is projected to fall back below present-day levels after 2050. Faster decarbonisation would bring that recovery sooner.
Why diesel emissions matter
Diesel vehicles, especially heavy-duty trucks and agricultural machinery, are among the largest sources of NOx emissions.

In many regions, heavy-duty diesel vehicles alone account for more than 70% of on-road NOx. These emissions not only directly harm pollinators. Through their effects on ozone, they also alter the chemical environment around flowers.

Electric vehicles produce zero tailpipe NOx. Replacing diesel vehicles with electric alternatives, particularly in freight, construction and farming, would cut an important source of NOx and, over time, help reduce the ozone pollution that interferes with floral scents. The benefits would be even greater as electricity generation becomes cleaner.

Our analysis shows that the rate of pollinator recovery will depend heavily on how quickly we reduce these emissions. Delaying the phase-out of diesel vehicles would prolong the mid-century ozone peak and delay the ecological recovery we all need.

Protecting pollinators should be considered a co-benefit of clean air and climate policy. Accelerating the transition from diesel to zero-emission vehicles, especially in heavy-duty and agricultural sectors where diesel remains important, would reduce a major source of NOx.

We also need better monitoring and research. Our evidence mostly comes from European studies on bees and a few other pollinator groups. We urgently need more research in high-pollution, biodiversity-rich regions, and on a wider range of pollinators including moths, flies and beetles.

The timing and location of pollution reductions could also matter. Measures that reduce exposure during peak flowering, for example, could help limit the disruption to pollinators before longer-term reductions in ozone kick in.
The fossil fuel transition is not just about carbon and climate. It is also about restoring the chemical cues that pollinators depend on as they search for flowers.
If we move quickly enough, we can shorten the difficult mid-century period and give bees, butterflies and the crops they support a genuine chance to recover.

The science is clear: cleaner air means healthier pollinators and more resilient food systems. Electric vehicles are one powerful tool in that toolkit. The sooner we deploy them at scale, the better the outlook for the insects that help feed us all.
James Ryalls has received funding from The Royal Society, British Ecological Society and UKRI.

articles.title: Air conditioners contribute to climate change – this 40-year-old treaty aims to limit the harm
articles.author: Matt Rigby, Reader in Atmospheric Chemistry, University of Bristol
paras: As temperatures broke records this summer, sales of air conditioning units soared. But this technology can compound climate change.

Air conditioners pump a gas, known as a refrigerant, around a sealed loop to carry heat out of (and sometimes into) the room. Some of that gas inevitably leaks out over the unit’s working life and when it is scrapped. Unfortunately, many refrigerants are potent greenhouse gases. Worldwide, leaked refrigerants account for roughly one-third of the climate impact of cooling, with electricity used to run the equipment responsible for the rest.

Air conditioning units have different labels. One that has recently been installed in a house or office probably says “R-32”, a type of hydrofluorocarbon (HFC). Older units often say “R-410A”, which is a blend of HFCs. Kilogram for kilogram, R-410A traps around 2,000 times more heat than carbon dioxide. R-32 is still a potent greenhouse gas, but only about a third as warming as R410A.

Scientists have been concerned about these refrigerants for decades. But if you wind the clock back to the 1970s and 1980s, they were more worried about the fact that they harmed the ozone layer than about their impact on the climate. Around this time, researchers discovered that the most widely used refrigerants back then, chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) were damaging the stratospheric ozone that shields us from the ultraviolet radiation that causes skin cancer.
Following the discovery of a “hole” in the ozone layer over Antarctica, nations agreed to sign a landmark environmental treaty known as the Montreal protocol in 1987.

This protocol and its later amendments phased out the CFCs, but allowed, as an interim measure, compounds called hydrochlorofluorocarbons (HCFCs) that were less harmful for the ozone layer. During the 1990s, HCFCs began to be replaced by HFCs, which don’t deplete ozone at all.
Without the Montreal protocol, studies suggest that ozone holes could have developed over the Arctic as well as Antarctica. Instead, the ozone layer is starting to recover.

Problem solved? Unfortunately not. HFCs, like CFCs and HCFCs, are incredibly potent greenhouse gases. Projections suggest that, without controls, they could add 0.3–0.5°C to global temperatures by the end of this century, a substantial fraction of the roughly 1.2°C of warming caused by human activities.

On October 15 2016, the parties to the Montreal protocol came together in Kigali, Rwanda. They agreed to phase down HFC production in favour of gases with lower global warming potentials (a measure of how potent the gas is relative to carbon dioxide). For the first time, this protocol was used to control gases purely because of their effect on the climate.

In 2014, two years before the Kigali amendment to the Montreal protocol was agreed, the EU adopted rules to phase down HFCs. These rules enable Europe and the UK to meet their Kigali commitments. Since January 2025, new small split air conditioners (units that heat or cool a single room) sold in the UK can no longer use R-410A, an HFC with high global warming potential. Portable units have been barred from using gases with high warming potential since 2020. The EU now aims to phase out HFCs almost entirely by 2050.
Beyond looking at labels on air conditioners, how do scientists like us know whether the Kigali amendment is working? The most direct test is to measure the atmosphere.

At Mace Head, an atmospheric research station on the windy west coast of Ireland, instruments have been measuring these gases continuously since 1987. Mace Head is one of a handful of stations around the world measuring these gases at concentrations of just a few parts per trillion.

In 2019, these measurements helped pinpoint the source of renewed global production of CFCs, years after the Montreal protocol’s ban. After a crackdown on illegal CFC production for use in insulating foams, emissions dropped.

The atmospheric data shows that the abundance of HFC compounds has increased substantially in the last decade. But overall growth in their emissions has slowed, and HFC emissions are substantially lower than those projected before the Kigali amendment was agreed.

A 2025 study projected that the climate impact of air conditioning could be similar to, or lower than, its impact today, even with a major increase in demand. But this depends on us meeting or exceeding our Kigali commitments, making air conditioners more efficient, expanding the use of zero-energy cooling measures (such as shading) and switching to low-carbon electricity.
Keeping a close eye on concentrations
Despite the apparent early success of the Kigali amendment, the atmospheric data show there can be no room for complacency.

Last year, scientists showed that emissions of a waste gas called HFC-23, the most potent climate warmer of all the HFCs, are far higher than the emissions of the gas officially reported by signatories to the Kigali amendment. Because HFC-23 is such a strong greenhouse gas, the discrepancy equates to just over half of the UK’s annual greenhouse gas emissions. Researchers and governments are now trying to figure out the reasons for the unexpected emissions.

The contents of air conditioners and fridges have been shaped by the Montreal protocol for almost 40 years. We know where it has worked, and where it needs closer scrutiny, only because researchers keep measuring the atmosphere. The challenge now is to maintain and expand that monitoring, so that the Kigali amendment can continue this remarkable legacy.

Matt Rigby receives funding from UK Research and Innovation and Horizon Europe. He is a Professor at the University of Bristol and a visiting Senior Research Scientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

Lucy Carpenter receives funding from UK Research and Innovation and Horizon Europe. She is a Professor at the University of York and co-chair of the Scientific Assessment Panel of the Montreal Protocol.

articles.title: California is taking a beating from an unusually destructive 2026 Pacific hurricane season
articles.author: Nicholas Grondin, Assistant Professor of Environmental Studies, University of Tampa
paras: California isn’t a place most Americans associate with tropical weather, but it’s taking a beating in 2026 from one of the most active eastern Pacific hurricane seasons in modern history.

For the second time ever, national forecasters issued a tropical storm watch for Southern California as Tropical Storm Rachel headed toward the region, bringing high tides, coastal flooding and drenching rain from Oct. 9-11. The first tropical storm watch was issued just three years earlier, for Hurricane Hilary.

The U.S. occasionally sees heavy rain from the remnants of Pacific storms that pass over Mexico and travel into the U.S. Southwest. But the 2026 season has been different. Three hurricanes deluged Hawaii as they passed close to the islands, a rare event for that state. And in September, Hurricane Marie churned up big waves that damaged oceanfront homes near Los Angeles before veering away from the coast.

Rachel weakened to an extratropical cyclone before its landfall in Baja California, but it brought high waves to Southern California that damaged more coastal homes and flooded streets. Its rainfall drenched communities from San Diego to the desert Southwest and even triggered flooding in Las Vegas.
I study Pacific hurricanes. While tropical storm impacts to California are unusual, they aren’t unprecedented. El Niño raises the risks.
California’s history with tropical storms
Historically, Southern California has seen a few direct hits from tropical storms and numerous cases of damage from systems that remained offshore.

To find the earliest known storm there, we have to travel back all the way to 1858, when a Category 1 hurricane, simply known as the 1858 San Diego Hurricane, brushed the coast of San Diego County and brought tropical-storm-force winds to the region. San Diego of the 1850s had a fraction of the population it has today, but the storm still caused significant damage.

While weaker than the 1858 hurricane, the only tropical storm known to have made landfall on the California coast was a 1939 tropical storm that hit Long Beach, in Los Angeles County. It brought tropical-storm-force winds across a large swath of Southern California, along with over 4 inches of rain in some areas.

That storm was a surprise, and the United States Weather Bureau – the precursor to the modern National Weather Service – opened a Southern California office in 1940 in response. A 2004 research paper hypothesized that if a similar storm hit the region in the mid-2000s, it would have likely caused over US$200 million in damage to the region.

While a few other tropical storms in the 1970s came close to a landfall in California, all weakened or changed course, avoiding a direct hit. This includes the remnants of Hurricane Hilary in 2023 that were still strong enough to cause widespread flooding in Southern California and dump 10 inches of rain in the mountains.
A handful of additional systems that made landfall in Baja California or stayed offshore have brought tropical-storm-force winds to the state, including Hurricane Nora in 1997.

In addition, multiple recent storms over the open ocean have generated swells that damaged port and pier infrastructure in the region, including hurricanes Marie in 2024, Narda in 2025 and another Marie in 2026.
El Niño raises California’s storm risk
Several environmental factors increase the probability of tropical storms making an approach to Southern California.

The most notable is El Niño. This natural climate pattern, defined by unusually warm water in the eastern tropical Pacific, increases the frequency of storms in the eastern North Pacific. That’s because warmer than normal sea surface temperatures in the region are necessary to support the formation and development of these storms.

Even during El Niño years, the waters off the coast of Southern California and northern Baja California are typically too cool to support hurricanes. Still, storms moving fast enough or with enough support from upper-level winds can survive these slightly cooler temperatures, allowing the system to make an approach toward California.

When Tropical Storm Rachel began its approach toward Southern California on Oct. 9, the National Hurricane Center noted that the sea surface temperatures were anomalously warm off the coast of Baja California and played a role in its potential to remain a tropical cyclone as it approached the coast.
The big storm problem: Rain
Like most eastern Pacific tropical storms and hurricanes, the primary effect on California from these systems is rainfall.

Most of Southern California is arid and rarely receives rainfall during summer and early fall. Early reports showed Rachel dumped upward of 6 inches of rain in parts of Southern California, including over 1 inch at San Diego International Airport in one weekend. That inch of rain in San Diego is double the typical October precipitation there.

While those amounts may seem minuscule compared to what typically comes with a tropical storm or hurricane landfall in places like Florida, they can cause flash flooding in the normally dry Southwest. The National Hurricane Center warned of flash flooding in California and other parts of the Southwest before Rachel’s landfall.
Unique cases like Rachel show that Mother Nature can always go against conventional wisdom, and, given enough time and the right conditions, potentially destructive things can happen.

articles.title: 300 glaciers have disappeared from the American West since the mid-20th century – the survivors have a few things in common
articles.author: Andrew Fountain, Professor of Geography, Portland State University
paras: From an airplane, most of the glaciers of the Rocky Mountain West look like small patches of white nestled into rugged landscape where the topography folds. The white is the snow cover, and lower down you can see the gray-blue bare ice.

In the middle of the 20th century, over 1,450 glaciers could be found in the contiguous U.S. Together, they covered 217 square miles (562 square kilometers) in six western states. Today, a comprehensive review my colleagues and I just published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences shows their total area has shrunk by 35% and they are still shrinking, perhaps faster.
A little more than 300 glaciers have disappeared, way more than I had anticipated.

Those that survive reflect just how vulnerable mountain glaciers have become as global temperatures rise. Where glaciers once covered large expanses of the western mountains thousands of years ago, most of the remaining glaciers in the Rockies and Sierra Nevada are small and found in topographically protected places.
Where US glaciers are disappearing fastest

When people think of glaciers, they often picture huge ice streams with icebergs calving off the front, like you’ll find in Alaska or Greenland. In the Lower 48 states, with the exception of a few large glaciers in Washington, they’re much smaller.

We found that the average glacier area is about one-tenth of a square mile (about a quarter of a square kilometer) in size. The area of the largest glacier, found on Washington’s Mount Rainier, is about 4.3 square miles (11.24 square kilometers).

I was surprised to find that glaciers in the Rocky Mountains – those in Colorado, Montana and Wyoming and in the Sierra Nevada of California – subsist because of their unique position on the landscape, which somewhat insulates them from the otherwise less-favorable regional climate.

The surviving Rocky Mountain glaciers inhabit shaded niches less exposed to direct sunshine and gain additional snow from avalanches. If these glaciers were exposed to more sun and less snow accumulation, they likely wouldn’t exit at all.
We found the fastest-thinning glaciers are in the Beartooth-Absaroka Mountains of the Rockies in southern Montana, which are losing about 1.5 feet (about half a meter) of ice thickness per year.

It’s a different story in Washington, where the glaciers on Mount Rainier and Mount Baker are much larger, have cooler summers and get a lot more snowfall. Although they too are shrinking, they do so at a much slower rate, about half a foot of ice thickness per year. The glacier area on Mount Rainier alone is greater than the total sum in all the other states.

In Washington, generally speaking, the higher you go, the less glacier loss you find. That makes sense; it’s cooler at higher elevations. But in the Rocky Mountain region there is no similar trend, suggesting the survivors are niche glaciers that depend on local topographic benefits.

In a study a few years ago, colleagues and I modeled the glaciers on Washington’s Olympic Peninsula and found most would disappear by 2070 under current climate trends. That indicates that glaciers elsewhere are probably not far behind.

The Olympics are vulnerable because they’re close to the Pacific Ocean at somewhat lower elevation. The other Washington glaciers, particularly on Mount Rainier and Mount Baker, will likely survive past 2100, but how much longer is an open question.
That raises a few concerns.

The principal importance of the glaciers is to provide water to high alpine ecosystems. The glaciers partially melt in late summer, providing cool water for cold-adapted fish and other stream life. They provide a water supply that’s otherwise absent in the dry late summer, after the seasonal snow disappears, when the region doesn’t get a lot of rain.
While the glaciers of the Rockies are primarily important for ecosystems at this point, those in Washington also contribute to hydropower production.

An important hazard is also associated with the glaciers on the steep-sided volcanoes of the Cascade Range, which stretches from California to Washington. The moraines formed by these glaciers are large, partly due to the highly erodible volcanic rock beneath the ice. Moving ice deposits eroded rocks, forming aprons at their lower ends. As the glaciers retreat, they leave the accumulated rocks behind as steep-sided moraines that are no longer buttressed by the ice.

High water flows from rain or glacier melt can undercut the moraines, triggering landslides and creating debris flows that go rocketing down the mountains. This happened in 2006 on Mount Hood and Mount Rainier and closed a number of highways. We’ll see that happen more often as the glaciers retreat.
The shrinking and eventual loss of all of these glaciers will affect ecosystems across the West, as well as waterways humans and wildlife rely on.
Andrew Fountain receives funding from the US Forest Service.

articles.title: How much rain can a hurricane make, and does the storm size matter?
articles.author: Zachary Handlos, Atmospheric Science Educator, Georgia Institute of Technology
paras: Curious Kids is a series for children of all ages. If you have a question you’d like an expert to answer, send it to CuriousKidsUS@theconversation.com.
How much rain can a hurricane make, and how much do big versus small hurricanes make? – Naarah, age 8, Pittsburgh
Hurricanes can produce enormous amounts of rain, adding up to trillions of gallons of water. But the big risk isn’t their total amount – it’s how much rain falls on each location.

One town in Texas got over 60 inches (152 centimeters) of rain from Hurricane Harvey over five days in 2017. That means empty swimming pools there would have filled with rainwater 5 feet (1.5 meters) deep. Hurricane Lane dumped 58 inches (147 centimeters) of rain on Kahuna Falls, Hawaii, the following year.
So, what causes that much rain, and does the size of the storm matter?

I’m an atmospheric scientist who teaches college students about weather at Georgia Tech. Let’s take a look at where a hurricane’s rainfall comes from and some of the questions about hurricanes and their rainfall that scientists are still trying to answer.
First, what goes into creating a hurricane?
A few ingredients are needed for a hurricane to form: A tropical thunderstorm complex, lots of moisture in the air, winds that don’t change speed much with height, and warm sea surface waters below.
The water temperature is very important.

The magic number for surface water temperature to be able to fuel a hurricane is at least 80 degrees Fahrenheit (26.5 degrees Celsius). At that temperature and above, the warm ocean water evaporates into the air, changing from liquid to vapor. As it makes that change, it provides energy to fuel the storm and also adds moisture to the atmosphere that eventually falls as rain.
When a hurricane moves over warm water, especially when the warm water extends many feet below the surface, the storm pulls in even more energy and moisture.
What affects hurricane size and rainfall?
This is one of the many questions about hurricanes that atmospheric scientists are working on.
The average hurricane is about 300 miles (482 kilometers) wide, but hurricanes – or typhoons, as they’re called in the western Pacific of the Northern Hemisphere – can be much bigger or smaller.

Super Typhoon Tip in 1979 grew to half the size of the lower 48 U.S. states. It had a radius of about 690 miles (1,110 kilometers), measured from the center of the storm to its outer edges, meaning it was 1,380 miles (2,222 kilometers) wide. Tropical Storm Marco’s gale-force winds in 2008, in comparison, had a radius of 11.5 miles (18.5 kilometers), meaning it was about 23 miles (37 kilometers) across – not much larger than New York City.

In 2025, scientists published a study showing that hurricane size appears to be influenced by how warm the ocean water is compared to its usual temperature that time of year. So, if a hurricane moves over water that is much warmer than normal, it tends to grow in size rapidly as well as growing in strength.

A recent hurricane that was very large in size was the extremely destructive Hurricane Helene in 2024. As Helene moved over water near Florida that was much warmer than normal for late September, it picked up lots of moisture that it carried all the way to the mountains of North Carolina. Several days of rain from the storm caused catastrophic flooding there.
But don’t count the small hurricanes out.
Just because a hurricane is small, that does not mean that it won’t have a big impact.

Hurricane Andrew in 1992 was destructive yet small. Its strongest winds extended only about 90 miles (150 km) from its center when it reached Miami and the Everglades. But that Category 5 hurricane is still known as one of the strongest hurricanes to hit the United States. It destroyed more than 25,000 homes.

A strong storm isn’t necessary for a lot of rain to fall. Tropical Storm Allison in 2001 is still one of the wettest tropical weather events in U.S. history. It caused over US$4 billion in damage in Texas alone, and it didn’t even develop into a hurricane!
So, what really leads to the highest rainfall totals?

Hurricanes that move slowly or nearly stop along their path usually cause the biggest rainfall problems because their rain keeps falling over the same location. The rain may be just as intense in a fast-moving hurricane, but it doesn’t stick around as long.

An example is Hurricane Harvey, which hit southeastern Texas in late August 2017. The storm dropped an estimated 27 trillion gallons of water over the state – that’s enough to fill about 40 million Olympic-size swimming pools.

When Harvey stalled over the Houston area, the storm kept drawing moisture from the warm waters of the Gulf. Over four days, it brought precipitation that totals as high as 60.58 inches (1.54 meters) of rain over Nederland, Texas. The extreme rainfall overran the town’s drainage and transformed Nederland into an island.
If a storm moves fast, like Hurricane Michael did in 2018 when it hit the Florida Panhandle, its winds and storm surge can make a big mess, but its rainfall totals will be lower.

Michael was a Category 5 hurricane – more powerful than Harvey and Helene – but its rainfall totals for locations along its path ranged from 6 to 10 inches (15 to 25 centimeters) because it was moving so fast. That’s still a lot of rain, but not compared to Harvey or to Helene, which dumped 30 inches (76 centimeters) of rain on Busick, N.C., over a few days.
So, a hurricane can be large or small in size and still have a big impact, depending on how slowly it’s moving.

There is still a lot to learn about hurricanes. Some big questions involve what’s known as rapid intensification. That occurs when a tropical storm’s maximum wind speed increases quickly, by 30 knots (about 34.5 miles per hour or 55 kilometers per hour) or more within 24 hours.
When rapid intensification occurs, as happened with hurricanes Harvey, Michael and Helene before they hit land, the storm can surprise coastal residents and become catastrophic.

Hurricanes of all sizes can be dangerous, so accurate forecasting well before they reach land is crucial to help people prepare for their impacts. One very important area of research that today’s scientists – and future scientists – can work on is improving forecasting so coastal residents know what’s coming and have time to prepare.

Hello, curious kids! Do you have a question you’d like an expert to answer? Ask an adult to send your question to CuriousKidsUS@theconversation.com. Please tell us your name, age and the city where you live.
And since curiosity has no age limit – adults, let us know what you’re wondering, too. We won’t be able to answer every question, but we will do our best.

Dr. Zachary Handlos is the Director of the Atmospheric and Oceanic Sciences undergraduate degree program and is a Senior Academic Professional within the School of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences at the Georgia Institute of Technology. He receives funding from the U.S. National Science Foundation, and is currently finishing his 2-year term as chair of the American Meteorological Society Board on Higher Education.

articles.title: Physics Nobel highlights Antarctica’s role in exploring the cosmos
articles.author: Daniella McCahey, Assistant Professor of History, Texas Tech University
paras: When Belgian American particle physicist Francis Halzen was awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in physics “for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin,” it was a reminder that for more than a century, scientists have treated Antarctica’s environments as windows onto worlds beyond Earth.

Antarctica has offered scientists a means of reaching and researching beyond Earth without leaving it. Various harsh and challenging Antarctic environments have served as testing sites for equipment destined for the Moon, Mars and beyond. Its ice has collected meteorites that arrive from extraterrestrial sources. And it is one of the best places on Earth from which to observe the universe.
Antarctica as an extraterrestrial-type place
Since the start of the 20th century, scientists have drawn parallels between Antarctic environments and those that can be found beyond our planet.
In 1901, the Australian physicist Louis Bernacchi compared being in Antarctica to what he thought it would be like on the Moon: “a dead silent world above you, and a dead silent world at your feet.”

By the mid-20th century, Antarctic environments were frequently used as approximations of extraterrestrial worlds. NASA officials traveled to the Antarctic “because this was as close to lunar conditions as we could get here on Earth,” as one of them, Ernst Stuhlinger, put it in 1968.

In preparation for the Viking mission to Mars in 1975-76, several microbiologists conducted research in the McMurdo Dry Valleys, convinced that this region of Antarctica closely resembled Mars. This type of research continues today.

Scientists continue to test technologies created for space exploration in the Antarctic, including spacesuits, robotics, and food production facilities, hoping that success in the Antarctic environment will translate into success in the more extreme environments of space.

Likewise, Antarctic workers have been studied to learn about the psychological aspects of long-term isolation and small-group dynamics in stressful situations, another key aspect of space exploration. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967 was even modeled after the 1959 Antarctic Treaty, agreeing among nations how to share special spaces for scientific research.

While some critics have said Antarctica’s conditions are too different to serve as a terrestrial stand-in for outer space, the idea of Antarctica as a practice or training ground for space exploration remains a fertile ground for the imagination, both for scientists and the general public.

Antarctic meteorites offer scientists access to materials from the Moon, Mars and beyond without leaving Earth. The men of the 1911-1914 Australasian Antarctic Expedition, led by geologist Douglas Mawson, collected the first meteorite discovered in Antarctica.
Modern meteorite science in Antarctica can be dated to the 1970s, following the 10th Japanese Antarctic Research Expedition’s 1969 discovery of nine meteorites in the Yamato Mountains.

Meteorites come down all around the planet, but Antarctica’s blue-ice areas, which comprise about 1% of Antarctica’s surface ice, often in mountainous regions, are among the best places to look. In those areas, strong katabatic winds flowing fast downhill remove snow, exposing hard, translucent ice. Dark-colored meteorites are easily spotted in contrast with the light-blue ice. And blue-ice areas contain unusually high concentrations of meteorites, as rocks from outer space either land on the surface or emerge from within the ice after being transported by glacial movement.

In 1976, geologist William Cassidy established the United States’ formal efforts to search for meteorites in Antarctica. Geologist Ursula Marvin, a member of one of the program’s earliest expeditions, credited Antarctic environments with providing a special look at planetary geology: “While waiting for future space missions we have found an elegant means of significantly extending the range of planetary samples by making our yearly expeditions to Antarctica.”

That effort has yielded, for example, the first recognized meteorite from the Moon, as well as a meteorite from Mars, which sparked a media firestorm in the mid-1990s when some scientists suggested that it bore evidence of fossilized microbial life.
High summits and clear skies

Despite one early physicist complaining that “taking Astronomical observations” in Antarctica’s weather was “positively painful,” astronomical work has been conducted in Antarctica for over a century. The central regions of the Antarctic ice sheet have low winds, long winter darkness and an exceptionally clear, stable atmosphere. Those conditions give Earth-based instruments unusually favorable access to signals coming from the cosmos.
Since the 1990s, the continent has been a major center for astronomy research, hosting a wide range of sensors and telescopes.

In 2007, the U.S. began operating the South Pole Telescope, which measures cosmic microwave background radiation and the dark energy driving the acceleration of the expansion of the universe, and which helped make the first image of a black hole in 2019. In subsequent years, research stations operated by Japan, China, France and Italy have also constructed increasingly large optical telescopes to observe astronomical objects, including stars and planets.

Scientists also use a constellation of other instruments on the Antarctic Plateau, such as the Antarctic PENGUIn magnetometer array, initially installed in the 1990s, to study extreme space weather events and advance understanding of the near-Earth space environment.

Closer to the coast, Antarctica also hosts a suite of other astrophysical research programs, such as the long-running “CosRay” observatory. Starting in 1960 at McMurdo, a neutron monitor measured low-energy cosmic rays – charged particles from outside the solar system. The project is still running, having moved to a nearby South Korean station in 2017.
IceCube and the Nobel Prize
Based at the University of Wisconsin, IceCube is a major international collaborative project that involves “450 physicists from 58 institutions in 14 countries,” its website reports.

The project began in 1987 when Halzen conceived of the Antarctic Muon and Neutrino Detector Array, known as AMANDA. That project tested the ability to use the ice of the polar plateau as a key element of a telescope to see neutrinos. Those elementary particles, first detected experimentally in 1956, travel through space, interacting only rarely with electrons and atomic nuclei.

Constructed at the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station starting in 1993, AMANDA was made up of 677 optical sensors deployed on 19 strings embedded deep in the polar ice. The strings were installed by drilling holes with hot water, lowering the modules into the ice and allowing the holes to refreeze.

The sensors wait for these rare occasions when a neutrino collides with a proton or neutron and produces charged particles that emit a faint flash, known as Cherenkov radiation. After AMANDA successfully detected neutrinos, Halzen and others in 2001 made the case to expand the array to place sensors throughout roughly a cubic kilometer of the Antarctic ice sheet. That project, IceCube, was originally deployed between 2004 and 2011, funded largely by the National Science Foundation.

With the larger group of sensors, scientists can not only detect neutrinos, but they can also determine their direction, energy and type. This allows them to trace some neutrinos back to their sources far away in the universe.
IceCube helps scientists gain insights into questions regarding supernova events, galaxy formation, the Big Bang, dark matter and the properties of the neutrino itself.
As Halzen and countless other scientists have found over the years, Antarctica’s extreme conditions serve as a crucial gateway to understanding some of the greatest mysteries of the cosmos.
In 2016, Daniella McCahey received a grant from the National Science Foundation.
From 2021 to 2025 Jean was a European Commission Marie Curie Research Fellow.

articles.title: China and the EU could turn Morocco into a surprise global hub for electric vehicles
articles.author: Linda Calabrese, Senior Research Fellow in the International Economic Development Group, ODI Global
paras: China now makes more than seven in ten of the world’s electric cars. In 2024 it produced over 12 million, 1.25 million of which were exported, mainly to Europe.

The EU is worried about this – alarmed by cheap, state-subsidised Chinese vehicles flooding its market and threatening the 13 million jobs which depend on its own auto industry. So the bloc has spent the past two years building a system of tariffs and rules to keep Chinese cars at bay.
In 2024, it imposed extra duties of up to 35% on Chinese electric vehicles (EVs), on top of an existing 10% import tariff. So far though, the EU’s tactics have yielded limited results.
Chinese vehicle sales in Europe nearly doubled between 2024 and 2025.
And much of this sales volume is being driven by the EV powerhouse that is developing at speed in Morocco.
Chinese firms producing cars in Morocco avoid exposure to those EU tariffs, and have announced US$6 billion (£4.5 billion) of investment in battery and electric car component plants in the country.

As a production base, Morocco has plenty of other advantages too. Its deep-water port in Tangier is the largest in Africa and the Mediterranean. It is also surrounded by state-sponsored industrial zones built specifically for carmakers and their suppliers.
Like its neighbours, Morocco has a free trade agreement with the EU, but is the only north African country which has one with the US.
And crucially, it has a good supply of the critical minerals needed for making batteries for EVs, including around 70% of the world’s phosphate reserves and plenty of cobalt.

Nor is Morocco starting from scratch in the car manufacturing business. Cars are the country’s biggest export. Many Moroccan workers have been trained in automotive assembly thanks to two major car companies.

Renault and Stellantis (the owner of 14 car brands including Peugeot, Fiat and Alfa Romeo) form a manufacturing base in Morocco that exported US$17 billion in cars and parts in 2024. This made Morocco one of the EU’s largest automotive trading partners ahead of China.
Of the 560,000 vehicles Morocco produced in 2024, the vast majority were petrol and diesel models. Only around 50,000 were electric.

But a new wave of investment can help the industry shift to green. Recent multi-billion-euro commitments from Stellantis and Renault will expand EV and hybrid capacity. At the same time, Chinese investment is filling domestic gaps in cathode and battery cell production.
This transformation did not happen to Morocco by chance. The government has spent two decades laying the groundwork.

It has built “free zones”, areas where businesses can import, manufacture, process and re-export goods without paying normal taxes or customs duties. These include automotive “clusters”, including the Tanger “automotive city”.
This year, Morocco introduced a carbon tax to keep its exports compliant with EU rules.
So Morocco has been positioning itself to benefit from the EU tariffs. Whether Morocco actually gains from this boom depends on what kind of production Chinese firms undertake.

They could treat Morocco as a mere transit hub, sending goods through Morocco with minimal processing purely to evade tariffs. Brussels has already caught one such case, ruling in 2025 that aluminium wheels shipped from Morocco were being unfairly subsidised by Beijing.

Or they could do the opposite: build real factories, share technology, train local engineers and buy from Moroccan suppliers. This is what would turn the current boom into lasting green industrialisation, of the type that the African Union wants to encourage, linking African mineral reserves to clean-energy manufacturing.
But there are potential stumbling blocks which could prevent Morocco from benefiting from this new wave of investment in the long term.

First, the EU rules themselves may not last. Its tariffs on Chinese electric cars are set for only five years, and legal challenges are already underway. Second, the technology may remain in Chinese hands. And third, the geopolitical and climate context is so volatile that business plans could change very quickly.

On the plus side, Morocco has an established manufacturing footprint and government support. So the unintended consequences of EU trade policy could end up producing one of the biggest green industrialisation stories of the next decade.
